meta.rendering_note: Magnetic flux \( \Phi \), EMF \( \varepsilon \), self-inductance \( L \), mutual inductance \( M \), angular frequency \( \omega \) and all vectors (\( \vec B \), \( \vec v \), \( \vec l \)) are single unnested KaTeX spans; no raw Unicode math symbols (including the arrow) appear anywhere outside KaTeX; every coupling coefficient \( k \) stays within the range 0 to 1; every numeric answer terminates cleanly (exact multiples of \( \pi \) or square roots where stated) or is a clean power-of-ten value.

topics.name: Magnetic Flux and Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
topics.summary: Magnetic flux through a flat loop in a uniform field is \( \Phi=BA\cos\theta \), where \( \theta \) is the angle between \( \vec B \) and the loop's normal; its unit is the weber (Wb). Flux is largest when the field is along the normal and zero when the field lies in the plane of the loop. Faraday's law says that an EMF is induced whenever the flux linked with a circuit changes: \( \varepsilon=-N\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} \) for a coil of \( N \) turns. The flux can change because \( B \) changes, because the area changes, or because the angle changes, as in a rotating coil. What matters is the rate of change, not the size of the flux: a huge steady flux induces nothing. Every turn of a coil contributes equally, so the total EMF scales with \( N \). The charge driven through a circuit, \( q=\dfrac{N\Delta\Phi}{R} \), depends only on the total flux change, not on how quickly it happens. Flipping a coil through \( 180^\circ \) changes its flux by \( 2BA \), not \( BA \).
topics.worked_example:
A 100-turn coil has the flux through each turn change by 0.02 Wb in 0.1 s. Find the EMF.

\( |\varepsilon|=N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}=100\times\dfrac{0.02}{0.1}=20 \) V.
common_mistakes: Using the flux value instead of its rate of change to find the EMF.
Forgetting to multiply by the number of turns \( N \).
Measuring \( \theta \) from the plane of the loop instead of from its normal.
Taking the flux change for a \( 180^\circ \) flip as \( BA \) instead of \( 2BA \).
Thinking the charge that flows depends on how fast the flux changes.

topics.name: Lenz's Law and Motional EMF: Direction, Induced Force, Power, and Energy Conservation
topics.summary: Lenz's law fixes the direction of induced current: it always opposes the change in flux that causes it, not the flux itself. If the flux is increasing, the induced field points against it; if the flux is decreasing, the induced field points along it, trying to maintain it. This follows from energy conservation: an aiding current would create energy from nothing. A conductor moving through a field has a motional EMF \( \varepsilon=(\vec v\times\vec B)\cdot\vec l \), which reduces to \( Blv \) only when \( \vec B \), the rod and \( \vec v \) are mutually perpendicular; otherwise only the perpendicular component counts. The current in the moving rod feels a force \( F=BIl=\dfrac{B^2l^2v}{R} \) that opposes the motion, so an external agent must push along the motion with an equal force to keep the velocity constant. In that steady state the mechanical power \( Fv \) equals the electrical power \( I^2R \) dissipated as heat. A rod rotating about one end gives \( \tfrac12B\omega l^2 \).
topics.worked_example:
A 0.5 m rod moves at 2 m/s through a 1 T field in a 0.5 Ω circuit. Find the power needed.

\( \varepsilon=1\times0.5\times2=1 \) V, \( I=2 \) A.

\( F=BIl=1 \) N opposing motion, so \( P=Fv=2 \) W, which equals \( I^2R=2 \) W.
common_mistakes: Making the induced current oppose the present flux instead of its change.
Using the full speed in \( Blv \) when the velocity is tilted relative to \( \vec B \).
Having the magnetic force on the rod aid its motion.
Taking the mechanical power input as different from the \( I^2R \) dissipated in the steady state.
Forgetting the factor \( \tfrac12 \) for a rotating rod.

topics.name: Self-Inductance: Definition, Inductance of a Solenoid, and Energy Stored in an Inductor
topics.summary: Self-inductance \( L \) is the flux linkage of a coil per unit of its own current, \( L=\dfrac{N\Phi}{I} \), measured in henry (Wb per A). When the current changes, the coil develops a back-EMF \( \varepsilon=-L\dfrac{dI}{dt} \) that opposes the change in either direction: it holds back a rising current and sustains a falling one, so inductance acts like electrical inertia, the analogue of mass. For a long solenoid, \( L=\mu_0n^2Al \), where \( n=N/l \) is the number of turns per unit length, not the total number of turns; equivalently \( L=\dfrac{\mu_0N^2A}{l} \). Filling the solenoid with a core of relative permeability \( \mu_r \) multiplies \( L \) by \( \mu_r \). The energy stored in the magnetic field is \( U=\tfrac12LI^2 \). Inductors with no mutual coupling combine exactly like resistors: in series they add, and in parallel their reciprocals add. The back-EMF is also why a spark can jump when an inductive circuit is suddenly broken. Doubling the turns on a fixed length quadruples \( L \), while stretching a solenoid with fixed total turns lowers it.
topics.worked_example:
A solenoid has 500 turns over 0.5 m and area \( 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2 \). Find \( L \).

\( n=1000 \) per metre, so \( L=4\pi\times10^{-7}\times10^6\times10^{-3}\times0.5=2\pi\times10^{-4} \) H \( =0.2\pi \) mH.
common_mistakes: Substituting the total turns \( N \) for \( n=N/l \) in \( \mu_0n^2Al \).
Believing the back-EMF opposes only an increasing (or only a decreasing) current.
Combining inductors with the capacitor rules.
Dropping the \( \tfrac12 \) or forgetting to square \( I \) in \( \tfrac12LI^2 \).
Not converting mH to H before calculating.

topics.name: Mutual Inductance: Definition, Coefficient of Coupling, and Coupled Circuits
topics.summary: Mutual inductance \( M \) links two circuits: the flux linkage in coil 2 due to a current in coil 1 is \( N_2\Phi_2=MI_1 \), and a changing current in coil 1 induces \( \varepsilon_2=-M\dfrac{dI_1}{dt} \) in coil 2, even if coil 2 carries no current of its own. Mutual inductance is always reciprocal, \( M_{12}=M_{21}=M \), whatever the turns on each coil. \( M \) depends only on geometry (turns, size, separation, orientation) and the core material, not on the currents. For a short coil or inner solenoid inside a long solenoid, only the smaller area carries the shared flux: \( M=\mu_0n_1N_2A_2 \) or \( \mu_0n_1n_2A_{inner}l \). The coefficient of coupling \( k=\dfrac{M}{\sqrt{L_1L_2}} \) always lies between 0 and 1; \( k=1 \) means all flux of one coil links the other, and \( k \) near 0 occurs, for example, for coils with perpendicular axes. Winding both coils on a common core multiplies \( M \) by the core's relative permeability, and doubling the turns of one coil doubles \( M \) while leaving \( k \) unchanged.
topics.worked_example:
Two coils have \( L_1=0.25 \) H, \( L_2=1 \) H and \( k=0.8 \). The current in coil 1 changes at 10 A/s. Find the EMF in coil 2.

\( M=0.8\times\sqrt{0.25}=0.4 \) H, so \( |\varepsilon_2|=0.4\times10=4 \) V.
common_mistakes: Treating \( M_{12} \) and \( M_{21} \) as different when the turns differ.
Reporting a coupling coefficient greater than 1 or negative.
Using the outer solenoid's area instead of the inner area for the shared flux.
Forgetting \( k \) when finding \( M \) from \( L_1 \) and \( L_2 \).
Thinking an open coil 2 has no induced EMF.

topics.name: Eddy Currents and the AC Generator
topics.summary: Eddy currents are loops of induced current in bulk conductors exposed to a changing flux or moving through a field. By Lenz's law they always oppose the relative motion or flux change that produces them, giving a braking force and dissipating energy as heat. This underlies electromagnetic damping (dead-beat galvanometers), electromagnetic brakes, induction furnaces and cooktops, speedometers and energy meters. Where eddy currents are unwanted, as in transformer and motor cores, thin insulated laminations raise the resistance of the eddy loops and so reduce the loss; slots in a swinging plate do the same. An AC generator rotates an \( N \)-turn coil of area \( A \) at constant \( \omega \) in a field \( B \): the flux linkage is \( NBA\cos\omega t \) and the EMF is \( \varepsilon=\varepsilon_0\sin\omega t \) with peak \( \varepsilon_0=NBA\omega \). The EMF is largest when the flux is zero and zero when the flux is largest. A rotation rate \( f \) gives \( \omega=2\pi f \).
topics.worked_example:
A 50-turn coil of area \( 0.1\ \text{m}^2 \) rotates at 600 rev/min in 0.2 T. Find the peak EMF.

\( f=10 \) rev/s, \( \omega=20\pi \) rad/s.

\( \varepsilon_0=50\times0.2\times0.1\times20\pi=20\pi \) V.
common_mistakes: Reporting the peak flux linkage \( NBA \) as the peak EMF, dropping \( \omega \).
Using \( f \) or \( \pi f \) in place of \( \omega=2\pi f \).
Claiming eddy currents aid motion.
Claiming lamination increases eddy-current loss.
Placing the EMF maximum where the flux is maximum.

questions.topic: Magnetic Flux and Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
questions.question: What is the SI unit of magnetic flux \( \Phi \)?
questions.explanation:
Magnetic flux is \( \Phi=BA\cos\theta \), a field multiplied by an area.

So its unit is tesla times square metre, \( \text{T m}^2 \), which is named the weber (Wb).
questions.hint: Flux is field times area.
distractor_logic: Tesla is the unit of the magnetic field \( \vec B \) itself; flux also multiplies by area.
Henry is the unit of inductance (flux linkage per ampere), not of flux.
Divides the field by area instead of multiplying, inverting the definition of flux.

questions.topic: Magnetic Flux and Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
questions.question: A uniform field of 2 T passes normally through a flat loop of area \( 0.5\ \text{m}^2 \). What is the magnetic flux through the loop?
questions.explanation:
The field is along the normal, so \( \theta=0^\circ \).

\( \Phi=BA\cos 0^\circ=2\times0.5\times1=1 \) Wb.
questions.hint: Use \( \Phi=BA\cos\theta \) with \( \theta \) measured from the normal.
distractor_logic: Treats the field as lying along the plane of the loop; here \( \vec B \) is along the normal, so \( \theta=0^\circ \) and \( \cos\theta=1 \).
Divides \( B \) by \( A \) (2/0.5) instead of multiplying them.
Divides \( A \) by \( B \) (0.5/2) instead of multiplying them.

questions.topic: Magnetic Flux and Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
questions.question: A square loop of area \( A \) lies with its plane parallel to a uniform field \( \vec B \). The flux through it is:
questions.explanation:
If the plane is parallel to \( \vec B \), the normal is perpendicular to \( \vec B \), so \( \theta=90^\circ \).

\( \Phi=BA\cos90^\circ=0 \): no field lines pass through the loop.
questions.hint: Find the angle between \( \vec B \) and the loop's normal.
distractor_logic: Assumes the maximum flux; that happens only when \( \vec B \) is along the normal, not along the plane.
Picks a halfway value as if the loop were tilted at \( 60^\circ \) to the field direction.
Uses \( \cos 45^\circ \), as though the loop were tilted halfway.

questions.topic: Magnetic Flux and Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
questions.question: Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction states that the induced EMF in a circuit is:
options: proportional to the magnetic flux linked with the circuit
equal to the rate of change of current in the circuit multiplied by its resistance
proportional to the square of the magnetic field strength
equal to the negative rate of change of magnetic flux linked with the circuit
questions.explanation:
Faraday's law: \( \varepsilon=-\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} \) for a single loop, and \( \varepsilon=-N\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} \) for \( N \) turns.

Only a changing flux produces an EMF; the minus sign expresses Lenz's law.
questions.hint: Think about what must happen to the flux for an EMF to appear.
distractor_logic: Ties EMF to the flux value rather than to how fast the flux changes; a large steady flux induces nothing.
Mixes Ohm's law with induction; induced EMF depends on flux change, not on resistance.
Invents a square-law dependence; induced EMF is linear in the rate of change of flux.

questions.topic: Magnetic Flux and Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
questions.question: A coil has \( N=100 \) turns. The flux through each turn changes by 0.02 Wb in 0.1 s. What is the magnitude of the average induced EMF?
questions.explanation:
\( |\varepsilon|=N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t} \).

\( |\varepsilon|=100\times\dfrac{0.02}{0.1}=100\times0.2=20 \) V.
questions.hint: Every turn contributes the same EMF, and they add.
distractor_logic: Uses the flux change per turn but forgets to multiply by the 100 turns.
Multiplies by \( N \) but forgets to divide by the time interval.
Reports the flux change per turn as if it were the EMF.

questions.topic: Magnetic Flux and Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
questions.question: In which situation is NO EMF induced in a closed conducting loop?
options: A bar magnet is pushed towards the loop
The loop is held at rest in a steady, uniform magnetic field
The loop is rotated in a steady, uniform magnetic field
The current in a nearby coil is switched off
questions.explanation:
An EMF needs a changing flux \( \Phi=BA\cos\theta \): a change in \( B \), \( A \) or \( \theta \).

For a loop at rest in a steady uniform field, none of these changes, so \( \dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}=0 \) and \( \varepsilon=0 \).
questions.hint: Check whether \( B \), \( A \) or \( \theta \) is changing.
distractor_logic: Moving a magnet towards the loop increases the flux through it, so an EMF is induced.
Rotation changes the angle between \( \vec B \) and the normal, so the flux changes.
Switching off the nearby current makes its flux through the loop fall to zero, which induces an EMF.

questions.topic: Magnetic Flux and Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
questions.question: A loop of area \( 0.5\ \text{m}^2 \) is in a uniform field of 0.4 T whose direction makes \( 60^\circ \) with the loop's normal. The flux through the loop is:
questions.explanation:
\( \Phi=BA\cos\theta \) with \( \theta=60^\circ \) from the normal.

\( \Phi=0.4\times0.5\times\tfrac12=0.1 \) Wb.
questions.hint: The angle is measured from the normal, so use cosine.
distractor_logic: Ignores the angle and uses \( \Phi=BA \).
Uses \( \sin60^\circ \) instead of \( \cos60^\circ \); the angle given is with the normal.
Divides \( B \) by \( A \) instead of multiplying.

questions.topic: Magnetic Flux and Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
questions.question: In Faraday's magnet-and-coil experiment, the galvanometer deflects while a magnet is pushed into a coil. If the magnet is then held stationary inside the coil, the galvanometer shows:
options: a steady deflection in the same direction
a steady deflection in the opposite direction
its maximum deflection, since the flux is now largest
questions.explanation:
With the magnet at rest, the flux through the coil is large but constant.

\( \dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}=0 \), so the induced EMF and current are zero.
questions.hint: Is the flux changing now?
distractor_logic: Assumes the current continues once the flux stops changing; induction needs a changing flux.
A reverse deflection needs a decreasing flux, e.g. pulling the magnet out, not holding it still.
Links EMF to the size of the flux rather than to its rate of change.

questions.topic: Lenz's Law and Motional EMF: Direction, Induced Force, Power, and Energy Conservation
questions.question: Lenz's law is a direct consequence of the conservation of:
questions.explanation:
If the induced current aided the change, it would increase the flux further, driving more current without any work being done.

That would create energy from nothing, so the induced current must oppose the change: this is Lenz's law, a statement of energy conservation.
questions.hint: What would go wrong if the induced current helped the change?
distractor_logic: Charge conservation is the basis of Kirchhoff's junction rule, not of the direction of induced current.
Momentum conservation does not fix which way an induced current flows.
Mass plays no role in electromagnetic induction.

questions.topic: Lenz's Law and Motional EMF: Direction, Induced Force, Power, and Energy Conservation
questions.question: A rod of length 0.5 m moves at 4 m/s in a 0.5 T field, with \( \vec B \), the rod and \( \vec v \) mutually perpendicular. The motional EMF across the rod is:
questions.explanation:
For mutually perpendicular \( \vec B \), \( \vec l \), \( \vec v \): \( \varepsilon=Blv \).

\( \varepsilon=0.5\times0.5\times4=1 \) V.
questions.hint: \( \varepsilon=Blv \).
distractor_logic: Leaves out \( B \), multiplying only \( l \) and \( v \).
Leaves out \( v \), multiplying only \( B \) and \( l \).
Divides \( v \) by \( Bl \) instead of multiplying.

questions.topic: Lenz's Law and Motional EMF: Direction, Induced Force, Power, and Energy Conservation
questions.question: The north pole of a bar magnet is moved towards a closed coil. The face of the coil nearer the magnet behaves like:
options: a south pole, attracting the approaching magnet
no pole at all, since current flows only once the magnet stops
a north pole, repelling the approaching magnet
a north pole, but only after the magnet has come to rest
questions.explanation:
The approach increases the flux through the coil.

The induced current opposes this change by making the near face a north pole, which repels the incoming north pole.
questions.hint: The coil opposes the approach.
distractor_logic: Reverses Lenz's law; attraction would aid the approach and create energy from nothing.
Current flows while the flux is changing, i.e. while the magnet moves.
Once the magnet is at rest the flux stops changing and the induced current vanishes.

questions.topic: Lenz's Law and Motional EMF: Direction, Induced Force, Power, and Energy Conservation
questions.question: The magnetic flux through a loop is directed into the page and is decreasing. The magnetic field produced by the induced current, inside the loop, points:
options: out of the page, to oppose the flux that is present
nowhere, since a decreasing flux induces no current
along the plane of the loop
into the page, to oppose the decrease
questions.explanation:
Lenz's law opposes the change in flux, not the flux itself.

The into-page flux is decreasing, so the induced current tries to maintain it by producing its own field into the page.
questions.hint: Ask whether the flux is growing or shrinking.
distractor_logic: Opposes the present flux direction instead of its change; for a decreasing flux the induced field supports the existing flux.
A decreasing flux is still a changing flux, so a current is induced.
The field of a current in a planar loop is along the normal inside the loop, not in its plane.

questions.topic: Lenz's Law and Motional EMF: Direction, Induced Force, Power, and Energy Conservation
questions.question: A metal rod slides to the right along two rails in a magnetic field, completing a circuit. The magnetic force on the rod due to the induced current is directed:
options: to the left, opposing the motion
to the right, aiding the motion
perpendicular to the rails, with no effect on the motion
zero, since the rod carries no net charge
questions.explanation:
The induced current flows through the rod, which lies in \( \vec B \), so it feels \( F=BIl \).

By Lenz's law this force opposes the cause, the rod's motion to the right, so it points left.
questions.hint: Induced effects oppose their cause.
distractor_logic: A force aiding the motion would speed the rod up and create energy from nothing, violating Lenz's law.
The force \( I\vec l\times\vec B \) on the rod lies along the rails, opposite to the velocity.
The force acts on the current in the rod, not on net charge; a current-carrying rod in \( \vec B \) feels \( BIl \).

questions.topic: Lenz's Law and Motional EMF: Direction, Induced Force, Power, and Energy Conservation
questions.question: The motional EMF across a conducting rod moving through a magnetic field arises because:
options: the magnetic field does work on the rod's free charges
the magnetic force \( q\vec v\times\vec B \) pushes free charges towards one end of the rod
the flux inside the rod's material changes
an electric field from the magnet's poles acts on the rod
questions.explanation:
Each free charge in the rod moves with velocity \( \vec v \) and feels \( q\vec v\times\vec B \) along the rod.

Charges pile up at one end until the resulting electric field balances this force, giving the EMF \( Blv \).
questions.hint: Think of the Lorentz force on the charges in the rod.
distractor_logic: The magnetic force is perpendicular to the charges' velocity, so on its own it does no work; the external agent supplies the energy.
A thin rod encloses no area; the EMF comes from the force on its moving charges.
A static magnet produces no electric field; the effect is purely magnetic.

questions.topic: Lenz's Law and Motional EMF: Direction, Induced Force, Power, and Energy Conservation
questions.question: A rod of length \( l \) moves along its own length, perpendicular to a uniform field \( \vec B \). The motional EMF across its ends is:
questions.explanation:
\( \varepsilon=(\vec v\times\vec B)\cdot\vec l \).

\( \vec v\times\vec B \) is perpendicular to \( \vec v \), and \( \vec l \) is along \( \vec v \), so the dot product is zero.
questions.hint: Check the direction of \( \vec v\times\vec B \) against the rod.
distractor_logic: Uses \( Blv \) without checking the geometry; \( \vec v \) is along \( \vec l \), so \( (\vec v\times\vec B)\cdot\vec l=0 \).
Halves the EMF with no basis; the rod-rotation factor of one half does not apply here.
Doubles the EMF with no basis.

questions.topic: Lenz's Law and Motional EMF: Direction, Induced Force, Power, and Energy Conservation
questions.question: A moving rod provides an EMF of 2 V to a circuit of total resistance 4 Ω. The electrical power dissipated is:
questions.explanation: \( P=\dfrac{\varepsilon^2}{R}=\dfrac{2^2}{4}=1 \) W.
questions.hint: \( P=\dfrac{\varepsilon^2}{R} \).
distractor_logic: Reports the current \( \varepsilon/R=0.5 \) A as the power.
Multiplies \( \varepsilon \) by \( R \) instead of using \( \varepsilon^2/R \).
Uses \( R/\varepsilon^2 \), inverting the formula.

questions.topic: Self-Inductance: Definition, Inductance of a Solenoid, and Energy Stored in an Inductor
questions.question: The henry, the SI unit of inductance, is equivalent to:
questions.explanation:
\( L=\dfrac{N\Phi}{I} \), so 1 H \( = \) 1 Wb per ampere.

Equivalently, from \( \varepsilon=L\dfrac{dI}{dt} \), 1 H \( = \) 1 V s per ampere.
questions.hint: Inductance is flux linkage per unit current.
distractor_logic: Multiplies flux by current instead of dividing; \( L=\dfrac{N\Phi}{I} \).
From \( \varepsilon=L\dfrac{dI}{dt} \), \( L \) is V s per A; this puts \( \text{s} \) and \( \text{A} \) the wrong way round.
That is the weber, the unit of flux, not of inductance.

questions.topic: Self-Inductance: Definition, Inductance of a Solenoid, and Energy Stored in an Inductor
questions.question: The current in a 2 H inductor changes at 3 A/s. The magnitude of the self-induced EMF is:
questions.explanation: \( |\varepsilon|=L\dfrac{dI}{dt}=2\times3=6 \) V.
questions.hint: \( \varepsilon=-L\dfrac{dI}{dt} \).
distractor_logic: Divides \( dI/dt \) by \( L \) instead of multiplying.
Adds \( L \) and \( dI/dt \) instead of multiplying.
Divides \( L \) by \( dI/dt \) instead of multiplying.

questions.topic: Self-Inductance: Definition, Inductance of a Solenoid, and Energy Stored in an Inductor
questions.question: A 4 H inductor carries a steady current of 2 A. The energy stored in its magnetic field is:
questions.explanation: \( U=\tfrac12LI^2=\tfrac12\times4\times2^2=8 \) J.
questions.hint: \( U=\tfrac12LI^2 \).
distractor_logic: Uses \( LI^2 \) and drops the factor \( \tfrac12 \).
Uses \( \tfrac12LI \), forgetting to square the current.
Squares \( L \) instead of \( I \) and drops the \( \tfrac12 \).

questions.topic: Self-Inductance: Definition, Inductance of a Solenoid, and Energy Stored in an Inductor
questions.question: The self-induced EMF in a coil:
options: opposes the current only while the current is increasing
opposes the current only while the current is decreasing
always opposes the current itself, even when it is steady
opposes any change in the current, whether the current is increasing or decreasing
questions.explanation:
\( \varepsilon=-L\dfrac{dI}{dt} \): the EMF depends on the rate of change of current.

It resists a rising current and sustains a falling one, acting like electrical inertia; for a steady current it is zero.
questions.hint: Look at the \( dI/dt \) in the formula.
distractor_logic: Forgets that a falling current is also opposed; the back-EMF then tries to keep it flowing.
Forgets that a rising current is also opposed; the back-EMF then holds it back.
A steady current means \( \dfrac{dI}{dt}=0 \), so there is no self-induced EMF at all.

questions.topic: Self-Inductance: Definition, Inductance of a Solenoid, and Energy Stored in an Inductor
questions.question: The self-inductance of a long solenoid of length \( l \), cross-sectional area \( A \) and \( n \) turns per unit length is:
options: \( \mu_0N^2Al \), with \( N \) the total number of turns
questions.explanation:
Field inside: \( B=\mu_0nI \). Flux linkage: \( N\Phi=(nl)(\mu_0nI)A \).

\( L=\dfrac{N\Phi}{I}=\mu_0n^2Al \), where \( n=N/l \).
questions.hint: \( n \) is turns per unit length, not total turns.
distractor_logic: Forgets to square \( n \); one factor comes from the field \( \mu_0nI \), another from the number of turns linked.
Substitutes the total turns \( N \) for \( n=N/l \); this overstates \( L \) by a factor of \( l^2 \).
Divides by \( l \) instead of multiplying; with \( n \) fixed, a longer solenoid has more turns and more inductance.

questions.topic: Self-Inductance: Definition, Inductance of a Solenoid, and Energy Stored in an Inductor
questions.question: Inductors of 2 H and 3 H are connected in series, far apart so there is no mutual coupling. The equivalent inductance is:
questions.explanation:
In series, the same current flows and the EMFs add: \( L\dfrac{dI}{dt}=L_1\dfrac{dI}{dt}+L_2\dfrac{dI}{dt} \).

So \( L_{eq}=L_1+L_2=5 \) H, just like resistors.
questions.hint: Inductors combine like resistors.
distractor_logic: Uses the reciprocal rule, which is how capacitors in series (or inductors in parallel) combine.
Multiplies the inductances instead of adding them.
Subtracts the inductances, as if their EMFs opposed.

questions.topic: Self-Inductance: Definition, Inductance of a Solenoid, and Energy Stored in an Inductor
questions.question: Inductors of 6 H and 3 H are connected in parallel with no mutual coupling. The equivalent inductance is:
questions.explanation:
In parallel, \( \dfrac{1}{L_{eq}}=\dfrac{1}{L_1}+\dfrac{1}{L_2}=\dfrac16+\dfrac13=\dfrac12 \).

\( L_{eq}=2 \) H, exactly as for resistors in parallel.
questions.hint: Parallel inductors behave like parallel resistors.
distractor_logic: Adds them as for series; that is the capacitor-style rule for parallel connection.
Takes the arithmetic mean, which has no basis.
Multiplies the inductances without dividing by their sum.

questions.topic: Self-Inductance: Definition, Inductance of a Solenoid, and Energy Stored in an Inductor
questions.question: In the analogy between mechanical and electrical systems, self-inductance plays the role of:
questions.explanation:
Mass resists changes in velocity, and inductance resists changes in current: \( \varepsilon=L\dfrac{dI}{dt} \) mirrors \( F=m\dfrac{dv}{dt} \).

Even the stored energies match: \( \tfrac12LI^2 \) and \( \tfrac12mv^2 \).
questions.hint: Compare \( L\dfrac{dI}{dt} \) with \( m\dfrac{dv}{dt} \).
distractor_logic: Current is the analogue of velocity, not inductance.
Force corresponds to EMF, the cause of changes in current.
Friction dissipates energy, like resistance; inductance stores energy without loss.

questions.topic: Mutual Inductance: Definition, Coefficient of Coupling, and Coupled Circuits
questions.question: The mutual inductance \( M \) of two coils is defined by the relation:
questions.explanation:
The flux linked with coil 2 is proportional to the current in coil 1.

The constant of proportionality is \( M \): \( N_2\Phi_2=MI_1 \).
questions.hint: Coil 2's flux is caused by coil 1's current.
distractor_logic: Divides by the current instead of multiplying; flux linkage grows with current.
Uses coil 2's own current, which defines self-inductance, not mutual inductance.
Squares the current; flux linkage is linear in current.

questions.topic: Mutual Inductance: Definition, Coefficient of Coupling, and Coupled Circuits
questions.question: For a pair of coils, the mutual inductance of coil 2 with respect to coil 1 is 5 mH. The mutual inductance of coil 1 with respect to coil 2 is:
options: 5 mH only if the coils have equal numbers of turns
questions.explanation:
Mutual inductance is reciprocal: \( M_{12}=M_{21}=M \).

So the answer is 5 mH.
questions.hint: Mutual inductance is a single shared quantity.
distractor_logic: Reciprocity \( M_{12}=M_{21} \) holds for any pair of coils, whatever their turns.
Takes the reciprocal of 5, as if the reverse coupling were inverse.
Doubles the value, as if the two directions added.

questions.topic: Mutual Inductance: Definition, Coefficient of Coupling, and Coupled Circuits
questions.question: Two coils have a mutual inductance of 2 H. The current in coil 1 changes at 3 A/s. The EMF induced in coil 2 is:
options: Zero, since coil 2 carries no current
questions.explanation: \( |\varepsilon_2|=M\dfrac{dI_1}{dt}=2\times3=6 \) V.
questions.hint: \( \varepsilon_2=-M\dfrac{dI_1}{dt} \).
distractor_logic: Divides the rate by \( M \) instead of multiplying.
Adds \( M \) and the rate.
The EMF in coil 2 arises from coil 1's changing current; coil 2 needs no current of its own.

questions.topic: Mutual Inductance: Definition, Coefficient of Coupling, and Coupled Circuits
questions.question: Which of the following is a possible value of the coefficient of coupling \( k \) between two coils?
questions.explanation:
\( k=\dfrac{M}{\sqrt{L_1L_2}} \), and always \( 0\le k\le1 \).

Only 0.6 lies in this range.
questions.hint: \( k \) lies between 0 and 1.
distractor_logic: Exceeds 1, which would need \( M>\sqrt{L_1L_2} \), impossible.
\( k \) is a ratio of magnitudes and cannot be negative.
Exceeds 1, impossible for any real pair of coils.

questions.topic: Mutual Inductance: Definition, Coefficient of Coupling, and Coupled Circuits
questions.question: A coefficient of coupling \( k=1 \) means that:
options: all the flux of one coil links the other coil
there is no magnetic coupling between the coils
the axes of the coils are perpendicular
questions.explanation:
\( k=1 \) is perfect coupling: \( M=\sqrt{L_1L_2} \).

It happens when every flux line of one coil passes through all turns of the other.
questions.hint: \( k=1 \) is the maximum possible coupling.
distractor_logic: That is \( k=0 \), the other extreme.
Perpendicular axes give almost no coupling, \( k \) near 0.
Perfect coupling gives \( M=\sqrt{L_1L_2} \), not the sum.

questions.topic: Mutual Inductance: Definition, Coefficient of Coupling, and Coupled Circuits
questions.question: The mutual inductance of two coils does NOT depend on:
questions.explanation:
\( M \) depends only on geometry (turns, size, separation, orientation) and the medium.

Currents change the flux, but \( M=\dfrac{N_2\Phi_2}{I_1} \) stays the same.
questions.hint: \( M \) is a property of the arrangement.
distractor_logic: More turns link more flux, so \( M \) increases with turns.
Moving the coils apart reduces the flux shared, lowering \( M \).
Turning one coil changes how much flux links it, so \( M \) changes.

questions.topic: Mutual Inductance: Definition, Coefficient of Coupling, and Coupled Circuits
questions.question: For two small coils placed near each other, the mutual inductance is smallest when:
options: they are coaxial and close together
one is wound directly over the other
their axes are parallel and they are side by side at small separation
questions.explanation:
With perpendicular axes, the field of one coil runs nearly parallel to the plane of the other.

Very little flux passes through it, so \( M \) is minimal.
questions.hint: Which arrangement shares the least flux?
distractor_logic: Coaxial, close coils share much of their flux, giving large \( M \).
Winding one over the other gives nearly perfect coupling.
Parallel, close coils still share a significant fraction of flux.

questions.topic: Mutual Inductance: Definition, Coefficient of Coupling, and Coupled Circuits
questions.question: Two coils have \( L_1=4 \) H, \( L_2=9 \) H and coefficient of coupling \( k=0.5 \). Their mutual inductance is:
questions.explanation: \( M=k\sqrt{L_1L_2}=0.5\times\sqrt{36}=0.5\times6=3 \) H.
distractor_logic: Multiplies \( k \) by \( L_1+L_2 \) instead of by \( \sqrt{L_1L_2} \).
Multiplies \( k \) by \( L_1L_2 \) without taking the square root.
Finds \( \sqrt{L_1L_2} \) but forgets to multiply by \( k \).

questions.topic: Eddy Currents and the AC Generator
questions.question: The iron core of a transformer or motor is made of thin, insulated laminations in order to:
options: reduce eddy-current losses by increasing the resistance of eddy-current paths
increase eddy-current losses so the core heats up faster
increase the magnetic flux through the core
make the core lighter, with no effect on losses
questions.explanation:
Eddy currents circulate in loops inside a solid core and waste energy as heat.

Thin insulated sheets restrict each loop to a tiny cross-section with high resistance, so the \( I^2R \) loss drops sharply.
questions.hint: What do the insulating layers do to the current loops?
distractor_logic: Reverses the purpose; lamination reduces, not increases, eddy-current heating.
Lamination does not raise the flux; the core material does that.
Weight is not the point; the insulated layers break up the eddy-current loops.

questions.topic: Eddy Currents and the AC Generator
questions.question: A copper plate swinging between the poles of a magnet comes to rest quickly. If several slots are cut in the plate, it will:
options: stop even more quickly, since the slots increase the eddy currents
swing for longer, since the slots reduce the eddy currents
swing exactly as before, since copper is non-magnetic
be pulled towards the magnet and stick to it
questions.explanation:
The motion induces eddy currents, which by Lenz's law oppose the motion, damping the swing.

Slots interrupt the current loops, so the braking is much weaker and the plate swings longer.
questions.hint: Slots block the circulating currents.
distractor_logic: Slots cut the paths of eddy currents, reducing them, not increasing them.
The damping comes from induced currents in the conductor, not from magnetism of copper.
Copper is not attracted by a magnet; the effect is a velocity-dependent braking force.

questions.topic: Eddy Currents and the AC Generator
questions.question: An AC generator has a 100-turn coil of area \( 0.02\ \text{m}^2 \) rotating at \( \omega=50 \) rad/s in a 0.1 T field. The peak EMF is:
questions.explanation:
\( \varepsilon_0=NBA\omega \).

\( \varepsilon_0=100\times0.1\times0.02\times50=10 \) V.
questions.hint: \( \varepsilon_0=NBA\omega \).
distractor_logic: Reports \( NBA \), the peak flux linkage, and drops the factor \( \omega \).
Uses \( BA\omega \), forgetting the 100 turns.
Halves the peak; the peak of \( \sin\omega t \) is 1.

questions.topic: Eddy Currents and the AC Generator
questions.question: Which of the following is an application of eddy currents?
questions.explanation:
An induction furnace uses a rapidly alternating field to induce large eddy currents in a metal charge.

Their heating melts the metal.
questions.hint: Which device heats metal without contact?
distractor_logic: Electrolysis is a chemical effect of current, not induction.
The filament is heated by a current supplied directly, not by induced eddy currents.
A solar cell converts light to electricity through the photovoltaic effect.

questions.topic: Eddy Currents and the AC Generator
questions.question: An AC generator works on the principle of:
options: electromagnetic induction, converting mechanical energy into electrical energy
the magnetic effect of current, converting electrical energy into mechanical energy
electrostatic induction, storing charge on plates
questions.explanation:
A coil rotated in a magnetic field has a changing flux, so an EMF is induced.

The mechanical work of turning the coil becomes electrical energy.
questions.hint: What makes the EMF appear in the rotating coil?
distractor_logic: That describes a motor, the reverse process.
Electrostatic induction describes charging by induction, not generation of AC.
Heating is a consequence of current, not how a generator produces it.

questions.topic: Eddy Currents and the AC Generator
questions.question: In an AC generator, the EMF is zero at the instant when the plane of the coil is:
options: parallel to \( \vec B \), so the flux through it is zero
perpendicular to \( \vec B \), so the flux through it is maximum
questions.explanation:
\( \Phi=NBA\cos\omega t \) and \( \varepsilon=NBA\omega\sin\omega t \).

When the flux is maximum (\( \cos\omega t=1 \)), \( \sin\omega t=0 \), so \( \varepsilon=0 \).
questions.hint: At maximum flux, the flux is momentarily not changing.
distractor_logic: That is the position of maximum EMF, where the flux changes fastest.
At \( 45^\circ \) the EMF is \( \dfrac{\varepsilon_0}{\sqrt2} \), not zero.
At this tilt the EMF is non-zero.

questions.topic: Eddy Currents and the AC Generator
questions.question: Electromagnetic brakes in some trains work because the eddy currents induced in the wheels or rails:
options: produce a force that aids the motion
only heat the rails, with no effect on motion
produce a force that opposes the relative motion
permanently reverse the field of the magnets
questions.explanation:
Relative motion between magnet and conductor induces eddy currents.

By Lenz's law these currents oppose the motion, giving a smooth braking force, and the kinetic energy becomes heat.
questions.hint: Induced effects always oppose their cause.
distractor_logic: A force aiding motion would violate Lenz's law and energy conservation.
The heating comes along with a real retarding force on the moving part.
The magnets' fields are unaffected; the eddy currents produce their own opposing field.

questions.topic: Eddy Currents and the AC Generator
questions.question: A generator coil rotates at 50 revolutions per second. Its angular frequency \( \omega \) is:
questions.explanation:
Each revolution is \( 2\pi \) radians.

\( \omega=2\pi f=2\pi\times50=100\pi \) rad/s.
questions.hint: \( \omega=2\pi f \).
distractor_logic: Uses the frequency in rev/s as if it were \( \omega \).
Uses \( \pi f \) instead of \( 2\pi f \).
Uses \( 2f \) and drops the \( \pi \).

questions.topic: Magnetic Flux and Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
questions.question: A single loop of area \( 0.04\ \text{m}^2 \) is placed normal to a field \( B=(0.2+0.5t) \) T, where \( t \) is in seconds. The induced EMF is:
questions.explanation:
\( \Phi=BA \), so \( \varepsilon=A\dfrac{dB}{dt} \).

\( \dfrac{dB}{dt}=0.5 \) T/s, so \( \varepsilon=0.04\times0.5=0.02 \) V.

The constant 0.2 T contributes no EMF because it does not change.
questions.hint: Only the changing part of \( B \) matters.
distractor_logic: Multiplies the area by the constant 0.2 T term instead of by the rate \( dB/dt=0.5 \) T/s.
Adds both coefficients (0.7) as if the constant part of \( B \) also induced EMF.
Uses \( dB/dt \) but forgets to multiply by the area.

questions.topic: Magnetic Flux and Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
questions.question: A flexible loop lies normal to a steady uniform field of 0.6 T. Its area increases at a constant rate of \( 0.05\ \text{m}^2 \) per second. The induced EMF is:
questions.explanation:
\( \Phi=BA \) with \( B \) constant, so \( \varepsilon=B\dfrac{dA}{dt} \).

\( \varepsilon=0.6\times0.05=0.03 \) V.
questions.hint: Flux can change through area as well as field.
distractor_logic: Assumes a steady field cannot induce EMF; a changing area changes the flux just as well.
Divides \( B \) by the area rate instead of multiplying.
Halves the result as though an average over the change were needed; the rate is constant.

questions.topic: Magnetic Flux and Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
questions.question: A coil of \( N=50 \) turns and area \( 0.02\ \text{m}^2 \) is in a 0.5 T field. It is turned from a position with its normal along \( \vec B \) to one with its normal perpendicular to \( \vec B \) in 0.1 s. The average induced EMF is:
questions.explanation:
Initial flux per turn \( =BA=0.5\times0.02=0.01 \) Wb; final flux \( =0 \).

\( |\varepsilon|=N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}=50\times\dfrac{0.01}{0.1}=5 \) V.
questions.hint: Find the flux at the start and at the end.
distractor_logic: Computes the per-turn EMF but forgets the factor of 50 turns.
Uses a flux change of \( 2BA \), which applies to a \( 180^\circ \) flip, not a \( 90^\circ \) turn.
Thinks the flux cannot change because the area is unchanged; the angle changes it.

questions.topic: Magnetic Flux and Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
questions.question: A 20-turn coil of area \( 0.1\ \text{m}^2 \) has its normal along a 0.5 T field. It is flipped through \( 180^\circ \) in 0.5 s. The average induced EMF is:
questions.explanation:
Flux per turn goes from \( +BA=+0.05 \) Wb to \( -BA=-0.05 \) Wb, a change of 0.1 Wb.

\( |\varepsilon|=20\times\dfrac{0.1}{0.5}=4 \) V.
questions.hint: After a flip, the flux points the other way.
distractor_logic: Takes the flux change as \( BA \); flipping reverses the flux, so the change is \( 2BA \).
Sees equal flux magnitudes at start and end and misses the sign reversal.
Uses the correct flux change per turn but forgets the 20 turns.

questions.topic: Magnetic Flux and Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
questions.question: The flux through a single loop rises uniformly from 0 to 6 Wb during 0 to 2 s, stays at 6 Wb from 2 s to 4 s, and falls uniformly to 0 from 4 s to 5 s. The EMF magnitudes during 2 to 4 s and during 4 to 5 s are:
questions.explanation:
EMF equals the slope of the flux-time graph.

From 2 s to 4 s the flux is constant, so \( \varepsilon=0 \).

From 4 s to 5 s, \( |\varepsilon|=\dfrac{6}{1}=6 \) V.
questions.hint: Look at the slope, not the height, of the graph.
distractor_logic: Assumes the 3 V from the rising phase continues while the flux is steady.
Links EMF to the flux value (6 Wb) instead of its slope, and reads no EMF where the flux changes.
Uses 2 s for the fall instead of the actual 1 s.

questions.topic: Magnetic Flux and Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
questions.question: A 100-turn coil of total resistance 10 Ω is linked with a flux that changes by 0.01 Wb per turn. How much charge flows through the coil?
options: It cannot be found without knowing the time taken
questions.explanation:
\( I=\dfrac{\varepsilon}{R}=\dfrac{N}{R}\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} \), so \( q=\int I\,dt=\dfrac{N\Delta\Phi}{R} \).

\( q=\dfrac{100\times0.01}{10}=0.1 \) C.
questions.hint: Integrate the current over time; the time cancels.
distractor_logic: Leaves out the factor of 100 turns in the flux linkage.
Multiplies the flux-linkage change by \( R \) instead of dividing.
Misses that \( q=\dfrac{N\Delta\Phi}{R} \) is independent of how fast the change happens.

questions.topic: Magnetic Flux and Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
questions.question: The field through a 200-turn coil of area \( 0.01\ \text{m}^2 \) (normal to the field) falls uniformly from 0.8 T to 0.2 T in 0.3 s. The induced EMF is:
questions.explanation:
\( \Delta B=0.6 \) T, so \( \Delta\Phi=0.6\times0.01=0.006 \) Wb per turn.

\( |\varepsilon|=200\times\dfrac{0.006}{0.3}=4 \) V.
questions.hint: \( \varepsilon=NA\dfrac{\Delta B}{\Delta t} \).
distractor_logic: Gets the per-turn EMF but forgets the 200 turns.
Finds the change in flux linkage but does not divide by the 0.3 s.
Leaves out the area, using only \( N\Delta B/\Delta t \).

questions.topic: Magnetic Flux and Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
questions.question: A single loop of area \( 0.05\ \text{m}^2 \) rotates at \( \omega=100 \) rad/s about an axis perpendicular to a 0.2 T field. The maximum induced EMF is:
questions.explanation:
\( \Phi=BA\cos\omega t \), so \( \varepsilon=BA\omega\sin\omega t \).

Maximum EMF \( =BA\omega=0.2\times0.05\times100=1 \) V.
questions.hint: Differentiate \( BA\cos\omega t \).
distractor_logic: Reports the peak flux \( BA \) instead of the peak EMF \( BA\omega \).
Picks the EMF at the instant of maximum flux, where the EMF is zero, not the maximum EMF.
Halves the peak value; the peak of \( \sin\omega t \) is 1.

questions.topic: Lenz's Law and Motional EMF: Direction, Induced Force, Power, and Energy Conservation
questions.question: A rod of length 0.2 m moves at a constant 5 m/s on rails in a 0.5 T field (all mutually perpendicular). The total circuit resistance is 0.5 Ω. The magnetic force on the rod is:
options: Zero, since the velocity is constant
questions.explanation:
\( \varepsilon=Blv=0.5\times0.2\times5=0.5 \) V and \( I=\dfrac{0.5}{0.5}=1 \) A.

\( F=BIl=0.5\times1\times0.2=0.1 \) N, opposing the motion; the external agent pushes forward with an equal 0.1 N.
questions.hint: Find the current first, then \( BIl \).
distractor_logic: Has the induced force aiding the motion, reversing Lenz's law.
Uses \( F=Il \) and forgets the factor \( B \).
Confuses the net force (zero, since the agent balances it) with the magnetic force alone.

questions.topic: Lenz's Law and Motional EMF: Direction, Induced Force, Power, and Energy Conservation
questions.question: A rod of length 0.5 m is kept moving at a constant 2 m/s through a 1 T field (mutually perpendicular) in a purely resistive circuit of 0.5 Ω. The mechanical power supplied by the external agent is:
options: 0 W, since no net work is done at constant velocity
questions.explanation:
\( \varepsilon=Blv=1\times0.5\times2=1 \) V, \( I=\dfrac{1}{0.5}=2 \) A.

Retarding force \( F=BIl=1\times2\times0.5=1 \) N, so \( P=Fv=2 \) W.

Check: \( I^2R=4\times0.5=2 \) W, equal to the mechanical input.
questions.hint: Mechanical power in equals electrical power dissipated.
distractor_logic: The net work is zero, but the agent still works against the magnetic retarding force.
Gives half the Joule heating; in steady state all the mechanical power becomes heat, not half of it.
Doubles the Joule heating; the input cannot exceed \( I^2R \) in this steady resistive case.

questions.topic: Lenz's Law and Motional EMF: Direction, Induced Force, Power, and Energy Conservation
questions.question: A rod of length 1 m lies perpendicular to a 0.4 T field. It moves at 5 m/s in a direction perpendicular to the rod but making \( 30^\circ \) with \( \vec B \). The motional EMF is:
questions.explanation:
\( |\vec v\times\vec B|=vB\sin30^\circ \), and this is along the rod.

\( \varepsilon=Blv\sin30^\circ=0.4\times1\times5\times\tfrac12=1 \) V.
questions.hint: Only the part of \( \vec v \) perpendicular to \( \vec B \) counts.
distractor_logic: Uses the full speed; only the velocity component perpendicular to \( \vec B \) contributes.
Uses \( \cos30^\circ \) instead of \( \sin30^\circ \); the velocity component along \( \vec B \) gives nothing.
Assumes any tilt kills the EMF; only motion exactly along \( \vec B \) would.

questions.topic: Lenz's Law and Motional EMF: Direction, Induced Force, Power, and Energy Conservation
questions.question: A metal rod of length 1 m rotates at \( \omega=20 \) rad/s about one end, in a plane perpendicular to a 0.5 T field. The EMF between its ends is:
questions.explanation:
A point at distance \( r \) moves at \( \omega r \), so \( d\varepsilon=B\omega r\,dr \).

\( \varepsilon=\int_0^lB\omega r\,dr=\tfrac12B\omega l^2=\tfrac12\times0.5\times20\times1=5 \) V.
questions.hint: Average speed of the rod is \( \omega l/2 \).
distractor_logic: Uses \( B\omega l^2 \) without the factor \( \tfrac12 \); points nearer the pivot move more slowly.
Uses \( \tfrac14 B\omega l^2 \), halving the correct result.
Thinks a rod enclosing no area has no EMF; each element cuts field lines.

questions.topic: Lenz's Law and Motional EMF: Direction, Induced Force, Power, and Energy Conservation
questions.question: A bar magnet, north pole down, falls through a horizontal ring. After it has passed through and is moving away below the ring, the induced current seen from above is:
options: zero, since the magnet has already passed
questions.explanation:
Below the ring, the magnet's field through the ring points downward (towards its south pole) and is decreasing.

The induced current opposes this decrease, so it makes a downward field inside the ring.

A downward field seen from above needs a clockwise current.
questions.hint: Is the downward flux increasing or decreasing?
distractor_logic: Opposes the present downward flux instead of its decrease; this reverses the correct sense.
The flux through the ring keeps changing as the magnet moves away, so a current still flows.
The flux decreases steadily as the magnet recedes, so the current keeps one direction.

questions.topic: Lenz's Law and Motional EMF: Direction, Induced Force, Power, and Energy Conservation
questions.question: A rod sliding on frictionless rails in a closed circuit in a uniform field is given a push and then released, with no external force afterwards. The rod:
options: keeps moving at constant velocity, since the rails are frictionless
slows down, with its kinetic energy appearing as heat in the circuit
speeds up, since the induced current pushes it forward
questions.explanation:
The moving rod drives a current, and the field exerts \( F=\dfrac{B^2l^2v}{R} \) on it, opposing motion.

The rod decelerates, and its kinetic energy becomes Joule heat \( I^2R \).
questions.hint: Which way does the induced force point?
distractor_logic: Ignores the magnetic retarding force \( BIl \) on the current-carrying rod.
Reverses Lenz's law; an accelerating rod would create energy from nothing.
The retarding force \( \dfrac{B^2l^2v}{R} \) shrinks with \( v \), so the rod slows gradually.

questions.topic: Lenz's Law and Motional EMF: Direction, Induced Force, Power, and Energy Conservation
questions.question: Suppose, contrary to Lenz's law, an induced current always aided the change in flux that produced it. What would follow?
options: Induced currents would simply be weaker than they are now
Nothing would change, since only the EMF's magnitude matters
A tiny change would grow without limit, producing energy without any work input
Induced currents would flow only in superconductors
questions.explanation:
An aiding current would increase the flux, which would induce more current, and so on.

This runaway would produce energy from nothing, so the induced current must oppose the change.
questions.hint: Follow the feedback loop.
distractor_logic: The problem is not the size of the current; aiding the change creates runaway growth.
The direction decides whether energy is conserved, so it matters greatly.
The material has nothing to do with it; the issue is energy conservation.

questions.topic: Lenz's Law and Motional EMF: Direction, Induced Force, Power, and Energy Conservation
questions.question: A rod of length 0.4 m and resistance 1 Ω moves at 10 m/s in a 0.5 T field (mutually perpendicular) on rails joined by a 3 Ω resistor. The current in the circuit is:
questions.explanation:
\( \varepsilon=Blv=0.5\times0.4\times10=2 \) V.

The rod and resistor are in series, total 4 Ω, so \( I=\dfrac{2}{4}=0.5 \) A.
questions.hint: The rod's own resistance is in series with the external resistor.
distractor_logic: Uses only the rod's 1 Ω and ignores the 3 Ω external resistor in series.
Halves the EMF as in the rotating-rod formula, which does not apply to translation.
Multiplies the EMF by the total resistance instead of dividing.

questions.topic: Self-Inductance: Definition, Inductance of a Solenoid, and Energy Stored in an Inductor
questions.question: A solenoid has 500 turns wound over a length of 0.5 m and a cross-sectional area of \( 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2 \). Taking \( \mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7} \) T m/A, its self-inductance is:
questions.explanation:
\( n=\dfrac{500}{0.5}=1000 \) per metre.

\( L=\mu_0n^2Al=4\pi\times10^{-7}\times10^6\times10^{-3}\times0.5=2\pi\times10^{-4} \) H.

That is \( 0.2\pi \) mH.
questions.hint: First find \( n=N/l \).
distractor_logic: Uses the total 500 turns in place of \( n=N/l=1000 \) per metre in \( \mu_0n^2Al \).
Leaves out the length \( l \) in \( \mu_0n^2Al \).
Divides by \( l \) instead of multiplying.

questions.topic: Self-Inductance: Definition, Inductance of a Solenoid, and Energy Stored in an Inductor
questions.question: The number of turns on a solenoid is doubled while its length and cross-section stay the same. Its self-inductance becomes:
questions.explanation:
\( L=\mu_0n^2Al \), and doubling the turns at fixed length doubles \( n \).

So \( L \) grows by \( 2^2=4 \).
questions.hint: \( L \) depends on \( n^2 \).
distractor_logic: Treats \( L \) as proportional to \( n \) instead of \( n^2 \).
Assumes inductance depends only on geometry, ignoring the number of turns.
Gets the direction of the effect wrong; more turns means more flux linkage per ampere.

questions.topic: Self-Inductance: Definition, Inductance of a Solenoid, and Energy Stored in an Inductor
questions.question: A 50 mH inductor carries a current of 4 A. The energy stored is:
questions.explanation:
\( L=0.05 \) H.

\( U=\tfrac12LI^2=\tfrac12\times0.05\times16=0.4 \) J.
questions.hint: Convert mH to H first.
distractor_logic: Uses \( \tfrac12LI \), not squaring the current.
Uses \( LI^2 \) and drops the \( \tfrac12 \).
Uses 50 in place of 0.05, not converting mH to H.

questions.topic: Self-Inductance: Definition, Inductance of a Solenoid, and Energy Stored in an Inductor
questions.question: The current in a 0.5 H coil falls uniformly from 4 A to zero in 0.2 s. The self-induced EMF is:
options: 10 V, acting against the original direction of the current
0.4 V, acting to keep the current flowing in its original direction
Zero, since the current ends at zero
10 V, acting to keep the current flowing in its original direction
questions.explanation:
\( |\varepsilon|=L\dfrac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}=0.5\times\dfrac{4}{0.2}=10 \) V.

The current is decreasing, so the back-EMF opposes the decrease by trying to keep the current flowing the same way.
questions.hint: The back-EMF opposes the change, not the current.
distractor_logic: Makes the EMF oppose the current itself rather than its change; a falling current is sustained, not pushed back.
Multiplies by \( \Delta t \) instead of dividing: \( 0.5\times4\times0.2 \).
The EMF depends on the rate of change during the fall, not on the final value.

questions.topic: Self-Inductance: Definition, Inductance of a Solenoid, and Energy Stored in an Inductor
questions.question: Three inductors of 2 H, 3 H and 6 H are connected in parallel with no mutual coupling. The equivalent inductance is:
questions.explanation:
\( \dfrac{1}{L_{eq}}=\dfrac12+\dfrac13+\dfrac16=\dfrac{3+2+1}{6}=1 \).

\( L_{eq}=1 \) H.
questions.hint: Add the reciprocals.
distractor_logic: Adds them as if in series.
Multiplies them together.
Takes the largest value as if it dominated.

questions.topic: Self-Inductance: Definition, Inductance of a Solenoid, and Energy Stored in an Inductor
questions.question: A 4 H inductor is connected in series with a parallel pair of 6 H and 12 H inductors, with no mutual coupling. The equivalent inductance is:
questions.explanation:
Parallel pair: \( \dfrac{1}{L_p}=\dfrac16+\dfrac1{12}=\dfrac14 \), so \( L_p=4 \) H.

In series with 4 H: \( L_{eq}=4+4=8 \) H.
questions.hint: Combine the parallel pair first.
distractor_logic: Adds all three as if they were in series.
Treats all three as if they were in parallel.
Adds 4 H to the average of 6 H and 12 H, which has no basis.

questions.topic: Self-Inductance: Definition, Inductance of a Solenoid, and Energy Stored in an Inductor
questions.question: At a certain instant, a 2 H inductor carries 3 A and the current is increasing at 4 A/s. The rate at which energy is being stored in the inductor is:
questions.explanation:
\( U=\tfrac12LI^2 \), so \( \dfrac{dU}{dt}=LI\dfrac{dI}{dt} \).

\( \dfrac{dU}{dt}=2\times3\times4=24 \) W.
questions.hint: Differentiate \( \tfrac12LI^2 \).
distractor_logic: Reports the back-EMF \( L\dfrac{dI}{dt}=8 \) V as a power.
Multiplies only \( L \) and \( I \).
Squares the current: \( LI^2\dfrac{dI}{dt} \).

questions.topic: Self-Inductance: Definition, Inductance of a Solenoid, and Energy Stored in an Inductor
questions.question: An air-cored solenoid has an inductance of 2 mH. It is completely filled with a core of relative permeability 500. The new inductance is:
questions.explanation:
Filling with a core replaces \( \mu_0 \) by \( \mu_r\mu_0 \), so \( L \) is multiplied by \( \mu_r \).

\( L=500\times2 \) mH \( =1000 \) mH \( =1 \) H.
questions.hint: \( L\propto\mu \).
distractor_logic: Assumes the core has no effect; it multiplies the flux by \( \mu_r \).
Divides by \( \mu_r \) instead of multiplying.
Multiplies correctly but forgets that 1000 mH is 1 H, not 1000 H.

questions.topic: Mutual Inductance: Definition, Coefficient of Coupling, and Coupled Circuits
questions.question: Two coaxial solenoids of length 0.5 m share the same axis. The inner has 1000 turns per metre and area \( 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2 \); the outer has 500 turns per metre and area \( 3\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2 \). Taking \( \mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7} \) T m/A, their mutual inductance is:
questions.explanation:
Only the inner area carries the shared flux: \( M=\mu_0n_1n_2A_{inner}l \).

\( M=4\pi\times10^{-7}\times1000\times500\times10^{-3}\times0.5=10^{-4}\pi \) H \( =0.1\pi \) mH.
questions.hint: Use the smaller (inner) area.
distractor_logic: Uses the outer area; the flux shared lies only within the inner solenoid's area.
Uses the total turns of each coil in place of turns per metre.
Leaves out the length \( l \).

questions.topic: Mutual Inductance: Definition, Coefficient of Coupling, and Coupled Circuits
questions.question: The current in coil 1 rises uniformly from 0 to 5 A in 0.1 s, inducing 2 V in coil 2. The mutual inductance is:
questions.explanation:
\( \dfrac{dI_1}{dt}=\dfrac{5}{0.1}=50 \) A/s.

\( M=\dfrac{|\varepsilon_2|}{dI_1/dt}=\dfrac{2}{50}=0.04 \) H \( =40 \) mH.
questions.hint: \( M=\dfrac{\varepsilon_2}{dI_1/dt} \).
distractor_logic: Divides the current rate by the EMF instead of the other way round.
Divides the EMF by the current change and forgets the time.
Multiplies the EMF by the rate instead of dividing.

questions.topic: Mutual Inductance: Definition, Coefficient of Coupling, and Coupled Circuits
questions.question: Two coils have \( L_1=2 \) mH, \( L_2=8 \) mH and \( M=2 \) mH. The coefficient of coupling is:
questions.explanation: \( k=\dfrac{M}{\sqrt{L_1L_2}}=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{16}}=\dfrac24=0.5 \).
questions.hint: Divide \( M \) by the geometric mean of the self-inductances.
distractor_logic: Divides \( M \) by \( L_1 \) alone.
Divides \( M \) by \( L_2 \) alone.
Inverts the ratio, giving a value above 1, which is impossible.

questions.topic: Mutual Inductance: Definition, Coefficient of Coupling, and Coupled Circuits
questions.question: A current of 2 A in coil A produces a flux linkage of 0.01 Wb in coil B. If instead a current of 4 A flows in coil B, the flux linkage in coil A is:
options: It cannot be found without the turns of each coil
questions.explanation:
\( M=\dfrac{0.01}{2}=0.005 \) H, and the same \( M \) works both ways.

Flux linkage in A \( =MI_B=0.005\times4=0.02 \) Wb.
questions.hint: Use the same \( M \) in reverse.
distractor_logic: Ignores the change in current from 2 A to 4 A.
Reports \( M \) (in henry) as the flux linkage.
Reciprocity \( M_{AB}=M_{BA} \) makes the turns unnecessary.

questions.topic: Mutual Inductance: Definition, Coefficient of Coupling, and Coupled Circuits
questions.question: Coil 2, of resistance 5 Ω, has mutual inductance 0.2 H with coil 1. The current in coil 1 changes at 50 A/s. The current induced in coil 2 is:
questions.explanation:
\( |\varepsilon_2|=M\dfrac{dI_1}{dt}=0.2\times50=10 \) V.

\( I_2=\dfrac{10}{5}=2 \) A.
questions.hint: Find the EMF, then use Ohm's law.
distractor_logic: Reports the induced EMF of 10 V as the current.
Divides \( R \) by \( \varepsilon \), inverting Ohm's law.
Divides \( M \) by \( R \), leaving out the rate of change.

questions.topic: Mutual Inductance: Definition, Coefficient of Coupling, and Coupled Circuits
questions.question: Two coils have self-inductances of 4 mH and 16 mH. The largest mutual inductance they could possibly have is:
questions.explanation:
\( M=k\sqrt{L_1L_2} \) with \( k\le1 \).

Maximum \( M=\sqrt{4\times16}=8 \) mH, at perfect coupling.
distractor_logic: Adds the self-inductances; \( M \) is limited by their geometric mean, not their sum.
Multiplies them without taking the square root.
Uses the arithmetic mean instead of the geometric mean.

questions.topic: Mutual Inductance: Definition, Coefficient of Coupling, and Coupled Circuits
questions.question: Coil 1 has 100 turns and coil 2 has 400 turns. A student claims that the mutual inductance of coil 2 due to coil 1 is four times that of coil 1 due to coil 2. The correct view is:
options: The claim is right, since coil 2 has four times the turns
\( M_{21} \) is actually one quarter of \( M_{12} \)
\( M_{21}=M_{12} \) always; the turn ratio cannot make them unequal
\( M_{21} \) is sixteen times \( M_{12} \), since turns enter squared
questions.explanation:
Mutual inductance is reciprocal for any pair of coils: \( M_{12}=M_{21}=M \).

Turns affect the size of \( M \), not its symmetry.
questions.hint: Mutual inductance is symmetric.
distractor_logic: More turns raise \( M \) for both directions equally; reciprocity still holds.
Reverses the student's error but keeps the false idea of asymmetry.
Squaring applies to self-inductance of one coil, and still would not break reciprocity.

questions.topic: Mutual Inductance: Definition, Coefficient of Coupling, and Coupled Circuits
questions.question: Two coils wound on an air core have a mutual inductance of 2 mH. Both are then wound on a common core of relative permeability 100 that carries all their flux. The mutual inductance becomes:
questions.explanation:
The core multiplies the field, and hence the shared flux, by \( \mu_r \).

\( M=100\times2 \) mH \( =200 \) mH.
questions.hint: \( M\propto\mu \), just like \( L \).
distractor_logic: Assumes the core has no effect on the shared flux.
Divides by \( \mu_r \) instead of multiplying.
Multiplies by \( \sqrt{\mu_r} \), as if only one coil benefited.

questions.topic: Eddy Currents and the AC Generator
questions.question: A 50-turn generator coil of area \( 0.1\ \text{m}^2 \) rotates at 600 revolutions per minute in a 0.2 T field. The peak EMF is:
questions.explanation:
\( f=\dfrac{600}{60}=10 \) rev/s, so \( \omega=2\pi\times10=20\pi \) rad/s.

\( \varepsilon_0=NBA\omega=50\times0.2\times0.1\times20\pi=20\pi \) V.
questions.hint: Convert rev/min to rad/s.
distractor_logic: Reports \( NBA \), the peak flux linkage, without the factor \( \omega \).
Uses 600 rev/min directly as \( \omega \) in rad/s.
Uses \( \omega=\pi f \) instead of \( 2\pi f \).

questions.topic: Eddy Currents and the AC Generator
questions.question: A generator's EMF is \( \varepsilon=\varepsilon_0\sin\omega t \) with \( \varepsilon_0=200 \) V. At the instant when \( \omega t=30^\circ \), the EMF is:
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon=200\sin30^\circ=200\times\tfrac12=100 \) V.
questions.hint: Substitute into \( \varepsilon_0\sin\omega t \).
distractor_logic: Uses \( \cos30^\circ \) instead of \( \sin30^\circ \).
Reports the peak value instead of the instantaneous value.
Uses \( \sin45^\circ \), the wrong angle.

questions.topic: Eddy Currents and the AC Generator
questions.question: Identical magnets are dropped through a vertical copper tube and through a PVC tube of the same size. Compared with the PVC tube, the magnet in the copper tube:
options: falls faster, because eddy currents pull it down
falls at the same rate, because copper is non-magnetic
falls more slowly, because eddy currents in the copper oppose its motion
stops and stays suspended inside the tube
questions.explanation:
The falling magnet changes the flux through rings of the copper tube, inducing eddy currents.

By Lenz's law these oppose the fall, so the magnet drops slowly; PVC is an insulator, so no current flows there.
questions.hint: Which tube can carry induced currents?
distractor_logic: Eddy currents oppose the motion; they cannot aid it.
The braking comes from induced currents in a conductor, not from any magnetism of copper.
The braking force needs motion; it balances gravity only at a non-zero terminal speed.

questions.topic: Eddy Currents and the AC Generator
questions.question: An induction cooktop heats a steel pan but not a glass dish placed on it. The reason is that:
options: glass reflects the magnetic field back into the cooktop
the cooktop surface itself becomes hot and only steel conducts that heat
steel is attracted to the coil, and the friction produces heat
eddy currents are induced only in the conducting steel, heating it
questions.explanation:
The coil below makes a rapidly alternating field that passes into the pan.

In a conductor this induces eddy currents whose \( I^2R \) heating warms the pan; glass is an insulator, so no current flows.
questions.hint: Heating needs a current to be induced.
distractor_logic: Glass does not reflect the field; it simply cannot carry induced currents.
The heat is generated in the pan by induced currents, not conducted from a hot surface.
There is no frictional heating; the heating is electrical, \( I^2R \).

questions.topic: Eddy Currents and the AC Generator
questions.question: If the rotation speed of a generator coil is doubled, with everything else unchanged:
options: the peak EMF doubles and the frequency doubles
the peak EMF stays the same and the frequency doubles
the peak EMF quadruples and the frequency doubles
the peak EMF doubles and the frequency stays the same
questions.explanation:
\( \varepsilon_0=NBA\omega \), so doubling \( \omega \) doubles \( \varepsilon_0 \).

One cycle of EMF happens per revolution, so the frequency also doubles.
questions.hint: \( \omega \) appears in both amplitude and frequency.
distractor_logic: Treats the peak EMF as \( NBA \), without the factor \( \omega \).
Squares the effect of \( \omega \); \( \varepsilon_0 \) is linear in \( \omega \).
The frequency of the AC equals the rotation frequency, so it also doubles.

questions.topic: Eddy Currents and the AC Generator
questions.question: A generator coil has a peak flux linkage \( NBA=0.5 \) Wb and rotates at \( \omega=100 \) rad/s. Its peak EMF is:
questions.explanation: \( \varepsilon_0=NBA\omega=0.5\times100=50 \) V.
questions.hint: Peak EMF is peak flux linkage times \( \omega \).
distractor_logic: Reports the peak flux linkage as the peak EMF, dropping \( \omega \).
Divides by \( \omega \) instead of multiplying.
Halves the peak, which has no basis.

questions.topic: Eddy Currents and the AC Generator
questions.question: A generator produces a peak EMF of 100 V at a frequency of 50 Hz. Its EMF as a function of time is:
questions.explanation:
\( \omega=2\pi f=100\pi \) rad/s.

So \( \varepsilon=\varepsilon_0\sin\omega t=100\sin(100\pi t) \) V.
questions.hint: Find \( \omega \) from \( f \).
distractor_logic: Uses the frequency directly as \( \omega \).
Uses \( \omega=\pi f \) instead of \( 2\pi f \).
Halves the peak value.

questions.topic: Eddy Currents and the AC Generator
questions.question: A moving-coil galvanometer whose coil is wound on a metallic frame comes to rest quickly after a deflection. This is because:
options: the metal frame adds mass, which alone stops the coil
eddy currents in the frame push the pointer further
the frame shields the coil from the magnetic field
eddy currents induced in the metal frame oppose the coil's motion
questions.explanation:
As the coil swings, the metal frame moves through the field and eddy currents are induced in it.

These oppose the motion, damping the oscillations so the pointer settles quickly (dead-beat).
questions.hint: The frame is a conductor moving in a field.
distractor_logic: Extra mass would make the coil swing longer, not stop sooner.
Eddy currents oppose the motion; they do not drive it further.
The coil still sits in the field; the frame provides damping, not shielding.

questions.topic: Magnetic Flux and Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
questions.question: A 50-turn square coil of side 0.1 m and total resistance 5 Ω is placed normal to a field that increases at 0.4 T/s. The induced current is:
questions.explanation:
Area \( =0.1^2=0.01\ \text{m}^2 \).

\( \varepsilon=NA\dfrac{dB}{dt}=50\times0.01\times0.4=0.2 \) V.

\( I=\dfrac{\varepsilon}{R}=\dfrac{0.2}{5}=0.04 \) A.
questions.hint: Square the side before using it.
distractor_logic: Uses the side 0.1 m as the area instead of \( 0.1^2=0.01\ \text{m}^2 \).
Forgets the factor of 50 turns.
Inverts Ohm's law, dividing \( R \) by \( \varepsilon \).

questions.topic: Magnetic Flux and Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
questions.question: A 500-turn coil of area \( 0.002\ \text{m}^2 \) and resistance 20 Ω lies normal to a 0.4 T field. It is quickly pulled completely out of the field. The charge that flows is:
options: It depends on how quickly the coil is pulled out
questions.explanation:
Change in flux linkage \( =NBA=500\times0.4\times0.002=0.4 \) Wb.

\( q=\dfrac{N\Delta\Phi}{R}=\dfrac{0.4}{20}=0.02 \) C.
questions.hint: Charge depends on the total change in flux linkage, not on time.
distractor_logic: Uses \( 2NBA \) as for a \( 180^\circ \) flip; removing the coil takes the flux from \( BA \) to 0 only.
Leaves out the 500 turns.
The charge equals \( \dfrac{N\Delta\Phi}{R} \), which does not depend on the speed of removal.

questions.topic: Magnetic Flux and Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
questions.question: A 10-turn coil of area \( 0.2\ \text{m}^2 \) has its normal at \( 60^\circ \) to a uniform field. The field grows uniformly from 0 to 0.5 T in 0.1 s. The average induced EMF is:
questions.explanation:
Final flux per turn \( =BA\cos60^\circ=0.5\times0.2\times\tfrac12=0.05 \) Wb.

\( |\varepsilon|=N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}=10\times\dfrac{0.05}{0.1}=5 \) V.
questions.hint: Only the component of \( \vec B \) along the normal gives flux.
distractor_logic: Ignores the \( 60^\circ \) angle and uses the full area.
Uses \( \sin60^\circ \) in place of \( \cos60^\circ \).
Forgets the factor of 10 turns.

questions.topic: Magnetic Flux and Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
questions.question: A copper ring and an identical wooden ring are placed in the same region where the magnetic flux through each is changing at the same rate. Which statement is correct?
options: An EMF and a current appear only in the copper ring
Equal currents flow in both rings
No EMF is induced in the wooden ring because wood is non-magnetic
Equal EMFs are induced in both rings, but a current flows only in the copper ring
questions.explanation:
Faraday's law gives \( \varepsilon=-\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} \), which is the same for both rings.

Current \( I=\dfrac{\varepsilon}{R} \): copper has low resistance so a current flows; wood's resistance is huge, so there is essentially none.
questions.hint: Separate EMF from current.
distractor_logic: EMF depends only on the rate of change of flux, not on the material; wood gets the same EMF.
Wood is an insulator, so its enormous resistance makes the current essentially zero.
Magnetic properties of the material play no role in the EMF; only \( \dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} \) matters.

questions.topic: Magnetic Flux and Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
questions.question: A coil rotates at constant angular velocity in a uniform field about an axis perpendicular to the field. At which orientation is the induced EMF largest?
options: When the plane of the coil is parallel to \( \vec B \), so the flux through it is zero
When the plane of the coil is perpendicular to \( \vec B \), so the flux through it is maximum
When the normal to the coil makes \( 45^\circ \) with \( \vec B \)
The EMF is the same at every orientation because \( \omega \) is constant
questions.explanation:
\( \Phi=NBA\cos\omega t \), so \( \varepsilon=NBA\omega\sin\omega t \).

\( \varepsilon \) is largest when \( \sin\omega t=1 \), i.e. when \( \cos\omega t=0 \): the flux is zero and changing fastest, with the coil's plane parallel to \( \vec B \).
questions.hint: EMF is largest where the flux changes fastest.
distractor_logic: Confuses maximum flux with maximum EMF; at maximum flux the flux is momentarily not changing.
At \( 45^\circ \) the EMF is only \( \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \) of its peak.
Constant \( \omega \) does not mean constant \( \dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} \); the flux varies sinusoidally.

questions.topic: Magnetic Flux and Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
questions.question: A 4-turn loop of resistance 2 Ω lies normal to a steady 1.5 T field. Its area shrinks uniformly from \( 0.3\ \text{m}^2 \) to \( 0.1\ \text{m}^2 \) in 0.5 s. The induced current is:
questions.explanation:
\( \Delta A=0.2\ \text{m}^2 \), so \( \Delta\Phi=1.5\times0.2=0.3 \) Wb per turn.

\( |\varepsilon|=4\times\dfrac{0.3}{0.5}=2.4 \) V.

\( I=\dfrac{2.4}{2}=1.2 \) A.
questions.hint: Use the change in area, then Ohm's law.
distractor_logic: Forgets the factor of 4 turns.
Reports the EMF of 2.4 V as the current, skipping the division by 2 Ω.
Uses the initial area \( 0.3\ \text{m}^2 \) instead of the change \( 0.2\ \text{m}^2 \).

questions.topic: Lenz's Law and Motional EMF: Direction, Induced Force, Power, and Energy Conservation
questions.question: A rod of length 0.4 m is pulled along rails by a constant 0.2 N force through a 0.5 T field (mutually perpendicular). The circuit resistance is 2 Ω and friction is absent. The terminal velocity is:
options: There is none; the rod keeps accelerating
questions.explanation:
At terminal velocity the retarding force equals the applied force: \( \dfrac{B^2l^2v}{R}=F \).

\( v=\dfrac{FR}{B^2l^2}=\dfrac{0.2\times2}{0.25\times0.16}=\dfrac{0.4}{0.04}=10 \) m/s.
questions.hint: Set the magnetic drag equal to the pull.
distractor_logic: Uses \( v=\dfrac{FR}{Bl} \), forgetting that both \( B \) and \( l \) appear squared.
Puts \( R \) in the denominator, \( v=\dfrac{F}{B^2l^2R} \).
Ignores the retarding force \( \dfrac{B^2l^2v}{R} \), which grows with \( v \) until it balances \( F \).

questions.topic: Lenz's Law and Motional EMF: Direction, Induced Force, Power, and Energy Conservation
questions.question: Horizontal rails carry a rod of length 0.5 m moving at 2 m/s along the rails. A uniform 0.4 T field makes \( 60^\circ \) with the vertical. The EMF across the rod is:
questions.explanation:
For a horizontal rod moving horizontally, \( (\vec v\times\vec B)\cdot\vec l \) picks out only the vertical component \( B\cos60^\circ=0.2 \) T.

\( \varepsilon=0.2\times0.5\times2=0.2 \) V.
questions.hint: Which component of \( \vec B \) is perpendicular to both \( \vec v \) and the rod?
distractor_logic: Uses the full \( B \); only the vertical component contributes for a horizontal rod moving horizontally.
Takes the \( \sin60^\circ \) component, which is the horizontal part that gives no EMF here.
Assumes a tilted field gives no EMF; the vertical component still does.

questions.topic: Lenz's Law and Motional EMF: Direction, Induced Force, Power, and Energy Conservation
questions.question: An isolated rod lies along the \( y \)-axis and moves with velocity along \( +x \) in a uniform field along \( +z \). Which end is at the higher potential?
options: Both ends are at equal potential, since no current can flow
The midpoint is higher than both ends
questions.explanation:
Force on a positive charge: \( q\vec v\times\vec B\propto\hat x\times\hat z=-\hat y \).

Positive charge accumulates at the \( -y \) end, making it the higher-potential end.
questions.hint: Work out \( \hat x\times\hat z \).
distractor_logic: Reverses the direction of \( \vec v\times\vec B \); \( \hat x\times\hat z=-\hat y \).
An open rod still has an EMF; charges separate until the electric field balances the magnetic force.
The force on charges is uniform along the rod, so potential varies steadily from end to end.

questions.topic: Lenz's Law and Motional EMF: Direction, Induced Force, Power, and Energy Conservation
questions.question: A metal rod of length 0.5 m rotates at 40 rad/s about one end in a plane perpendicular to a 0.2 T field. A 2 Ω resistor is connected between the pivot and the rotating tip through a sliding contact. The current is:
questions.explanation:
\( \varepsilon=\tfrac12B\omega l^2=\tfrac12\times0.2\times40\times0.25=1 \) V.

\( I=\dfrac{1}{2}=0.5 \) A.
questions.hint: Find the EMF of the rotating rod first.
distractor_logic: Uses \( B\omega l^2 \) without the factor \( \tfrac12 \).
Halves the EMF once more after applying \( \tfrac12B\omega l^2 \).
Multiplies the EMF by the resistance instead of dividing.

questions.topic: Lenz's Law and Motional EMF: Direction, Induced Force, Power, and Energy Conservation
questions.question: A 0.1 kg rod moving at 4 m/s on frictionless rails in a closed circuit in a magnetic field is left to itself until it stops. The total heat produced in the circuit is:
options: Zero, since no battery is present
questions.explanation:
The only energy available is the rod's kinetic energy, \( \tfrac12mv^2=\tfrac12\times0.1\times16=0.8 \) J.

The induced current slows the rod to rest, converting all of it into Joule heat.
questions.hint: Where does the rod's kinetic energy go?
distractor_logic: Assumes only half the kinetic energy becomes heat; all of it does.
Uses \( mv^2 \), forgetting the \( \tfrac12 \) in kinetic energy.
The rod itself is the source: its kinetic energy drives the current.

questions.topic: Lenz's Law and Motional EMF: Direction, Induced Force, Power, and Energy Conservation
questions.question: A square loop of side 0.1 m and resistance 0.5 Ω is pulled out of a 1 T field at a constant 2 m/s, with its plane perpendicular to the field. The work done in pulling it completely out is:
questions.explanation:
\( \varepsilon=Blv=1\times0.1\times2=0.2 \) V, \( I=\dfrac{0.2}{0.5}=0.4 \) A.

\( F=BIl=1\times0.4\times0.1=0.04 \) N over a distance of 0.1 m, so \( W=0.04\times0.1=4\times10^{-3} \) J.

Check: \( I^2Rt=0.16\times0.5\times0.05=4\times10^{-3} \) J.
questions.hint: Only one side of the loop is still in the field.
distractor_logic: Doubles the work, as if both vertical sides produced opposing forces; only the side in the field does.
Reports the force 0.04 N in joules instead of multiplying by the 0.1 m distance.
Halves the correct answer, as if only half the input became heat.

questions.topic: Self-Inductance: Definition, Inductance of a Solenoid, and Energy Stored in an Inductor
questions.question: A solenoid of 1000 turns, length 0.4 m and area \( 2\times10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2 \) has its current raised uniformly from 0 to 2 A in 0.01 s. Taking \( \mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7} \) T m/A, the back-EMF is:
questions.explanation:
