\( n=\dfrac{1000}{0.4}=2500 \) per metre, so \( L=\mu_0n^2Al=4\pi\times10^{-7}\times6.25\times10^6\times2\times10^{-4}\times0.4=2\pi\times10^{-4} \) H.

\( \dfrac{dI}{dt}=\dfrac{2}{0.01}=200 \) A/s.

\( |\varepsilon|=2\pi\times10^{-4}\times200=0.04\pi \) V.
questions.hint: Find \( L \) using \( n=N/l \), then \( L\dfrac{dI}{dt} \).
distractor_logic: Uses total turns \( N \) in place of \( n \) in \( \mu_0n^2Al \), giving too small an \( L \).
Reports the inductance value as the EMF, forgetting to multiply by \( \dfrac{dI}{dt} \).
Inserts a spurious \( \tfrac12 \) borrowed from the energy formula.

questions.topic: Self-Inductance: Definition, Inductance of a Solenoid, and Energy Stored in an Inductor
questions.question: To double the energy stored in an inductor, its current must be multiplied by:
questions.explanation:
\( U=\tfrac12LI^2\propto I^2 \).

For \( U \) to double, \( I^2 \) must double, so \( I \) scales by \( \sqrt{2} \).
questions.hint: Energy goes as current squared.
distractor_logic: Treats energy as proportional to \( I \); it goes as \( I^2 \).
Inverts the relation, squaring 2 instead of taking a square root.
Reduces the current, which would lower the stored energy.

questions.topic: Self-Inductance: Definition, Inductance of a Solenoid, and Energy Stored in an Inductor
questions.question: The current in a 0.2 H inductor is reduced from 5 A to 3 A. The energy released by the inductor is:
questions.explanation:
\( U_1=\tfrac12\times0.2\times25=2.5 \) J and \( U_2=\tfrac12\times0.2\times9=0.9 \) J.

Energy released \( =2.5-0.9=1.6 \) J.
questions.hint: Subtract the two stored energies.
distractor_logic: Uses \( \tfrac12L(\Delta I)^2 \); the energy change is \( \tfrac12L(I_1^2-I_2^2) \), not the square of the difference.
Drops the \( \tfrac12 \).

questions.question: Three identical 6 mH inductors, with no mutual coupling, can be connected in various ways. The maximum and minimum equivalent inductances obtainable are:
questions.explanation:
All in series gives the maximum: \( 6+6+6=18 \) mH.

All in parallel gives the minimum: \( \dfrac{6}{3}=2 \) mH.
questions.hint: Series adds, parallel divides.
distractor_logic: Swaps maximum and minimum, as happens when using the capacitor-style rules.
Takes the minimum as a single inductor, ignoring the all-parallel arrangement.
Uses only two of the three inductors in each case.

questions.topic: Self-Inductance: Definition, Inductance of a Solenoid, and Energy Stored in an Inductor
questions.question: In a 0.5 H inductor the current rises uniformly from 0 to 4 A in 2 s, stays at 4 A for 2 s, then falls uniformly to 0 in 1 s. The magnitudes of the self-induced EMF in these three intervals are:
questions.explanation:
Rise: \( 0.5\times\dfrac{4}{2}=1 \) V.

Steady: \( \dfrac{dI}{dt}=0 \), so 0 V.

Fall: \( 0.5\times\dfrac{4}{1}=2 \) V, opposite in sign to the first interval.
questions.hint: EMF follows the slope of the current graph.
distractor_logic: Gives an EMF in the steady interval, linking EMF to current rather than to its change.
Uses 2 s for the fall instead of 1 s.
Swaps the rise and fall rates.

questions.topic: Self-Inductance: Definition, Inductance of a Solenoid, and Energy Stored in an Inductor
questions.question: A solenoid's length is doubled while its total number of turns and cross-sectional area stay the same. Its self-inductance:
questions.explanation:
\( L=\mu_0n^2Al=\dfrac{\mu_0N^2A}{l} \) with \( n=N/l \).

With \( N \) and \( A \) fixed, \( L\propto\dfrac1l \), so doubling \( l \) halves \( L \).
questions.hint: Write \( L \) in terms of the total turns.
distractor_logic: Reads \( L=\mu_0n^2Al \) as proportional to \( l \) while forgetting that \( n \) halves.
Accounts for \( n^2 \) falling to one quarter but forgets the factor \( l \) doubling.
Assumes a fixed number of turns fixes the inductance.

questions.topic: Mutual Inductance: Definition, Coefficient of Coupling, and Coupled Circuits
questions.question: Two coils have \( L_1=0.25 \) H, \( L_2=1 \) H and \( k=0.8 \). The current in coil 1 changes at 10 A/s. The EMF induced in coil 2 is:
questions.explanation:
\( M=k\sqrt{L_1L_2}=0.8\times\sqrt{0.25}=0.8\times0.5=0.4 \) H.

\( |\varepsilon_2|=0.4\times10=4 \) V.
questions.hint: Find \( M \) from \( k \) first.
distractor_logic: Uses \( M=\sqrt{L_1L_2} \), ignoring \( k \).
Uses \( L_2 \) as if it were the mutual inductance.

questions.question: Two coils have \( L_1=0.2 \) H, \( M=0.3 \) H and \( k=0.75 \). The self-inductance \( L_2 \) is:
questions.hint: Rearrange \( k=\dfrac{M}{\sqrt{L_1L_2}} \).
distractor_logic: Stops at \( \sqrt{L_1L_2}=0.4 \) H without solving for \( L_2 \).
Uses \( \dfrac{M^2}{L_1} \), which assumes \( k=1 \).

questions.topic: Mutual Inductance: Definition, Coefficient of Coupling, and Coupled Circuits
questions.question: A student reports two coils with \( L_1=4 \) H, \( L_2=4 \) H and \( M=5 \) H. This result is:
options: impossible, because it gives \( k=1.25 \), exceeding 1
possible, since \( M \) can exceed the self-inductances when coils have many turns
impossible, because \( M \) must equal \( L_1+L_2 \)
questions.explanation:
\( k=\dfrac{M}{\sqrt{L_1L_2}}=\dfrac{5}{4}=1.25 \).

Since \( k \) can never exceed 1, \( M \) cannot exceed 4 H here.
questions.hint: Compute \( k \).
distractor_logic: Turns raise \( L_1 \) and \( L_2 \) too; \( M \) can never exceed \( \sqrt{L_1L_2} \).
Reciprocity always holds, so this is no escape.
\( M \) has an upper limit of \( \sqrt{L_1L_2} \), not a required value of \( L_1+L_2 \).

questions.topic: Mutual Inductance: Definition, Coefficient of Coupling, and Coupled Circuits
questions.question: A short coil of 100 turns and area \( 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2 \) is placed coaxially inside a long solenoid with 2000 turns per metre and area \( 4\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2 \). Taking \( \mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7} \) T m/A, their mutual inductance is:
questions.explanation:
Field inside the solenoid: \( B=\mu_0n_1I_1 \). Flux linkage of the short coil: \( N_2BA_2 \).

\( M=\mu_0n_1N_2A_2=4\pi\times10^{-7}\times2000\times100\times10^{-3}=8\pi\times10^{-5} \) H \( =0.08\pi \) mH.
questions.hint: The short coil's area sets the shared flux.
distractor_logic: Uses the solenoid's area; only the flux through the short coil's smaller area links it.
Halves the result as if the coil sat at the solenoid's end.
Doubles the result by adding \( M_{12} \) and \( M_{21} \), which are one and the same.

questions.topic: Mutual Inductance: Definition, Coefficient of Coupling, and Coupled Circuits
questions.question: When the current in coil 1 changes at 10 A/s, a self-induced EMF of 4 V appears in coil 1 and an EMF of 3 V appears in coil 2. If \( L_2=0.9 \) H, the coefficient of coupling is:
questions.hint: Find \( L_1 \) and \( M \) from the two EMFs.
distractor_logic: Divides \( M \) by \( L_1 \) alone.
Divides \( M \) by \( L_2 \) alone.

questions.topic: Mutual Inductance: Definition, Coefficient of Coupling, and Coupled Circuits
questions.question: For two coupled coils, the number of turns of coil 2 is doubled with everything else unchanged. Then:
options: \( M \) is unchanged and \( k \) halves
\( M \) doubles and \( k \) is unchanged
questions.explanation:
\( M\propto N_2 \), so \( M \) doubles; \( L_2\propto N_2^2 \), so \( L_2 \) quadruples.

\( k=\dfrac{M}{\sqrt{L_1L_2}} \) becomes \( \dfrac{2M}{2\sqrt{L_1L_2}} \), unchanged.
questions.hint: Track how \( M \) and \( L_2 \) each scale.
distractor_logic: Forgets that \( L_2 \) quadruples, so \( \sqrt{L_1L_2} \) also doubles.
Squares the turns factor for \( M \); \( M \) is linear in each coil's turns.
\( M \) depends on the flux linkage of coil 2, which doubles with its turns.

questions.topic: Eddy Currents and the AC Generator
questions.question: A generator produces \( \varepsilon=\varepsilon_0\sin\omega t \) with \( \varepsilon_0=200 \) V and frequency 50 Hz, starting from zero at \( t=0 \). The EMF at \( t=\dfrac{1}{600} \) s is:
questions.explanation:
\( \omega=2\pi\times50=100\pi \) rad/s.

\( \omega t=\dfrac{100\pi}{600}=\dfrac{\pi}{6} \), i.e. \( 30^\circ \).

\( \varepsilon=200\sin30^\circ=100 \) V.
questions.hint: Find the phase \( \omega t \) first.
distractor_logic: Uses \( \cos \) in place of \( \sin \) at the phase \( 30^\circ \).
Reports the peak value without working out the phase.
Treats so short a time as negligible, ignoring that \( \omega \) is large enough to make \( \omega t=30^\circ \).

questions.topic: Eddy Currents and the AC Generator
questions.question: A 100-turn coil of area \( 0.01\ \text{m}^2 \) rotates at 300 rev/min in a 0.5 T field. The coil's resistance is 2 Ω and it feeds an external 3 Ω resistor. The peak current is:
questions.explanation:
\( f=\dfrac{300}{60}=5 \) rev/s, so \( \omega=10\pi \) rad/s.

\( \varepsilon_0=NBA\omega=100\times0.5\times0.01\times10\pi=5\pi \) V.

\( I_0=\dfrac{5\pi}{2+3}=\pi \) A.
questions.hint: Total resistance is coil plus external.
distractor_logic: Divides by the coil's resistance only, ignoring the external resistor.
Divides by the external resistor only, ignoring the coil's own resistance.
Uses \( NBA \) instead of \( NBA\omega \) as the peak EMF.

questions.topic: Eddy Currents and the AC Generator
questions.question: A copper disc spinning freely between the poles of a strong magnet slows down and stops. Its lost kinetic energy appears mainly as:
options: energy stored in the magnet, strengthening it
gravitational potential energy of the disc
heat produced by eddy currents in the disc
electromagnetic radiation emitted by the magnet
questions.explanation:
The spinning disc cuts field lines, so eddy currents circulate in it.

They create a retarding torque (Lenz's law), and the kinetic energy is dissipated as \( I^2R \) heat in the disc.
questions.hint: Where do eddy currents deposit energy?
distractor_logic: The magnet's field is unchanged; it only provides the field in which currents are induced.
The disc stays at the same height, so its gravitational energy does not change.
No significant radiation is produced; the energy is dissipated resistively.

questions.topic: Eddy Currents and the AC Generator
questions.question: Which of the following changes would reduce eddy-current loss in a motor's iron core the most?
options: Replacing the laminated core with a solid block of the same iron
Increasing the frequency of the alternating flux
Using a core material with higher electrical conductivity
questions.explanation:
Eddy-current loss grows with the induced EMF and falls as the path resistance rises.

Thinner insulated laminations confine the loops to narrower, higher-resistance paths, so the loss falls.
questions.hint: Aim for smaller EMF or higher path resistance.
distractor_logic: A solid block offers large low-resistance loops, increasing the loss.
Faster flux changes induce larger EMFs and hence larger eddy currents.
Higher conductivity lets bigger eddy currents flow, increasing the loss.

questions.topic: Eddy Currents and the AC Generator
questions.question: Generator X has \( N \) turns and area \( A \), rotating at \( \omega \) in field \( B \). Generator Y has \( 2N \) turns and area \( A/2 \), rotating at \( 2\omega \) in the same field. The ratio of their peak EMFs \( \varepsilon_Y/\varepsilon_X \) is:
questions.explanation:
\( \varepsilon_0=NBA\omega \).

For Y: \( (2N)\,B\,(A/2)\,(2\omega)=2NBA\omega \), so the ratio is 2.
questions.hint: Multiply the scaling factors of \( N \), \( A \) and \( \omega \).
distractor_logic: Ignores the doubled \( \omega \), treating peak EMF as \( NBA \).
Forgets that the area is halved.
Halves instead of doubling, inverting the effect of \( \omega \).

questions.topic: Eddy Currents and the AC Generator
questions.question: A generator's peak EMF is \( 10\pi \) V. The average EMF over the half-cycle from \( \omega t=0 \) to \( \omega t=\pi \) is:
questions.explanation:
Average of \( \sin\omega t \) over \( 0 \) to \( \pi \) is \( \dfrac{2}{\pi} \).

\( \varepsilon_{avg}=\dfrac{2}{\pi}\times10\pi=20 \) V.

Equivalently, the flux linkage changes by \( 2NBA \) in half a period.
questions.hint: The average of \( \sin \) over half a cycle is \( 2/\pi \).
distractor_logic: That is the average over a full cycle; over this half-cycle the EMF keeps one sign.
Reports the peak instead of the average.
Uses the root-mean-square value, which is a different kind of average.

questions.topic: Magnetic Flux and Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
questions.question: A rod slides at 2 m/s along parallel rails 0.5 m apart, joined at one end, in a steady 0.4 T field normal to the plane of the rails. Using the rate of change of flux through the circuit, the induced EMF is:
options: Zero, since the field is steady
questions.explanation:
The enclosed area grows at \( lv=0.5\times2=1\ \text{m}^2 \) per second.

\( \varepsilon=B\dfrac{dA}{dt}=0.4\times1=0.4 \) V, the same as \( Blv \): motional EMF is Faraday's law applied to a growing circuit.
questions.hint: Find how fast the enclosed area grows.
distractor_logic: The field is steady, but the enclosed area grows, so the flux still changes.
Doubles the area growth rate as if both rails contributed separately.
Halves the result, as though averaging over the motion.

questions.question: A zero-resistance rod of length 1 m is moved at a constant 4 m/s through a 0.5 T field (mutually perpendicular) on zero-resistance rails joined by a pure 0.5 H inductor. Starting from zero current, the current after 2 s is:
options: Infinite at once, since there is no resistance
questions.explanation:
Motional EMF: \( \varepsilon=Blv=0.5\times1\times4=2 \) V.

With no resistance, \( L\dfrac{dI}{dt}=\varepsilon \), so \( \dfrac{dI}{dt}=\dfrac{2}{0.5}=4 \) A/s.

After 2 s, \( I=8 \) A.
questions.hint: The back-EMF balances the motional EMF.
distractor_logic: Reports the rate \( \dfrac{dI}{dt}=4 \) A/s as the current.
Multiplies \( \varepsilon \), \( L \) and \( t \) instead of using \( \dfrac{\varepsilon t}{L} \).
Ignores the inductor's back-EMF, which limits how fast the current can grow.

questions.question: Two coils with \( L_1=1 \) H and \( L_2=4 \) H are perfectly coupled (\( k=1 \)) and connected in series so their fluxes aid each other. The equivalent inductance is:
questions.explanation:
\( M=k\sqrt{L_1L_2}=\sqrt{4}=2 \) H.

Series aiding: \( L=L_1+L_2+2M=1+4+4=9 \) H.
questions.hint: Coupling adds \( 2M \) when fluxes aid.
distractor_logic: Ignores the coupling, using the uncoupled series rule.
Adds \( M \) only once; each coil's flux links the other, so it enters as \( 2M \).

\( \varepsilon=10\sin30^\circ=5 \) V.

Power \( =mgv=0.05\times10\times0.2=0.1 \) W, dissipated by eddy currents that brake the magnet (Lenz's law).

\( L=\dfrac{N\Phi}{I}=\dfrac{0.4}{4}=0.1 \) H.

questions.question: An aluminium ring rests on the iron core of a coil. When the coil is switched on, the ring jumps up. Why?
options: The ring is attracted to the coil and then bounces off it
Aluminium is strongly magnetised by the coil and repelled like a magnet
The growing flux induces a current in the ring that opposes the increase, so the ring is repelled
The ring is heated by the coil and rises by convection
questions.explanation:
The coil and ring are magnetically coupled: switching on makes the flux through the ring grow rapidly.

The induced current in the ring opposes this growth, so its field repels the coil's field and the ring is thrown up.

questions.question: A long straight wire carries an upward current that is decreasing. A square loop lies to its right, in the same plane. Viewed from the front, the induced current in the loop is:
options: zero, since the loop is at rest
questions.explanation:
To the right of an upward current, the field points into the page.

That into-page flux is decreasing, so the induced current tries to maintain it by making its own into-page field inside the loop.

An into-page field inside the loop needs a clockwise current.

questions.topic: Lenz's Law and Motional EMF: Direction, Induced Force, Power, and Energy Conservation
questions.question: When a switch carrying a large current through an inductive circuit is suddenly opened, a spark often jumps across the switch contacts. This happens because:
options: the sudden fall in current induces a large EMF that tries to keep the current flowing
the induced EMF opposes the current and pushes charge backwards across the gap
the switch contacts become magnetised and attract each other
the stored energy disappears instantly, so no EMF is involved
questions.explanation:
Opening the switch makes \( \dfrac{dI}{dt} \) very large, so \( \varepsilon=-L\dfrac{dI}{dt} \) is very large.

By Lenz's law this EMF opposes the decrease, driving current across the gap as a spark and releasing the stored energy \( \tfrac12LI^2 \).
questions.hint: Think of inductance as electrical inertia.
distractor_logic: Makes the EMF oppose the current rather than its decrease; it actually sustains the current.
Magnetisation of the contacts has nothing to do with the spark.
The stored energy \( \tfrac12LI^2 \) must go somewhere; it drives the spark.

questions.explanation:

questions.topic: Mutual Inductance: Definition, Coefficient of Coupling, and Coupled Circuits
questions.question: A metal detector has a transmitter coil carrying alternating current and a separate receiver coil. How does a buried metal object change the receiver's signal?
options: The metal blocks all flux, so the receiver EMF always drops to zero
Eddy currents induced in the metal create their own changing field, which induces an extra EMF in the receiver
The metal increases the transmitter current directly by contact
Eddy currents in the metal aid the transmitter's field, doubling it
questions.explanation:
The transmitter's changing field induces eddy currents in the metal.

These currents produce their own changing field, which is coupled (mutual inductance) to the receiver coil and alters the EMF it picks up.
questions.hint: The metal acts like a third coupled circuit.
distractor_logic: The metal does not block flux entirely; it adds its own induced field.
There is no electrical contact; the effect is purely inductive.
Eddy currents oppose the changing field that creates them, rather than aiding it.

questions.question: A square loop of side 0.2 m and resistance 1 Ω moves at 5 m/s into a region of uniform 0.5 T field much larger than the loop, with its plane perpendicular to the field. The EMF while entering and while fully inside is:
options: 0.5 V while entering, 0.5 V while fully inside
0 V while entering, 0.5 V while fully inside
0.5 V while entering, 0 V while fully inside
0.25 V while entering, 0 V while fully inside
questions.explanation:
While entering, the flux grows at \( Blv=0.5\times0.2\times5=0.5 \) V.

Fully inside, the flux is constant, so the net EMF is zero (both sides have equal, opposing motional EMFs).
questions.hint: When does the flux change?
distractor_logic: Fully inside, the flux is constant; the EMFs in the two sides cancel.
Reverses the phases; only entry changes the flux.
Halves the EMF with no basis.

questions.question: Two coaxial rings face each other. The current in ring 1 is decreasing. The force between the rings is:
questions.explanation:
Ring 2's flux (from ring 1) is decreasing, so its induced current flows in the same sense as ring 1's current to sustain it.

Parallel currents attract, so the rings pull together.
questions.hint: Decreasing flux: the induced current supports it.
distractor_logic: Has the induced current opposing the present flux; for a decreasing flux it supports it, giving attraction.
The changing coupled flux induces a current in ring 2, so there is a force.
The current decreases steadily, so the force does not reverse.

questions.question: A 50-turn coil is wound around the middle of a long solenoid with 1000 turns per metre and area \( 2\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2 \). The coil's own area is three times the solenoid's. Taking \( \mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7} \) T m/A, the mutual inductance is:
options: Zero, since the coil lies outside the solenoid
questions.explanation:
Flux through the outer coil is only the solenoid's flux: \( \Phi=\mu_0n_1I_1A_{sol} \).

\( M=\dfrac{N_2\Phi}{I_1}=4\pi\times10^{-7}\times1000\times50\times2\times10^{-3}=4\pi\times10^{-5} \) H \( =0.04\pi \) mH.
questions.hint: Where does the solenoid's field exist?
distractor_logic: Uses the coil's larger area; the solenoid's field is confined to its own cross-section.
The coil encloses the solenoid, so all the solenoid's flux passes through it.
Introduces a spurious \( \tfrac12 \).

questions.topic: Lenz's Law and Motional EMF: Direction, Induced Force, Power, and Energy Conservation
questions.question: A generator coil is kept rotating at a constant angular velocity while it supplies current to a lamp. Which statement is correct?
options: No torque is needed at constant angular velocity
An external torque must supply mechanical power equal to the electrical power delivered, because the induced current produces an opposing torque
Torque is needed only when no load is connected
The induced current produces a torque that helps the rotation
questions.explanation:
The current in the coil sits in \( \vec B \), so the coil feels a torque opposing its rotation (Lenz's law).

At constant \( \omega \) the driving torque balances it, and the mechanical power input equals the electrical power output.
questions.hint: Energy delivered must come from somewhere.
distractor_logic: Ignores the retarding torque from the current-carrying coil in the field.
With no load there is no current, so no retarding torque; the load is what demands the torque.
Reverses Lenz's law; an aiding torque would create energy from nothing.

Flux \( =B\cos60^\circ\times lx \), so \( \varepsilon=B\cos60^\circ\,lv \).

\( \varepsilon=0.8\times\tfrac12\times0.5\times3=0.6 \) V.
questions.hint: Only the normal component of \( \vec B \) gives flux.
distractor_logic: Ignores the tilt and uses the full field.
Uses \( \sin60^\circ \), the component lying in the plane, which gives no flux.
A tilted field still has a normal component that gives a changing flux.

questions.question: The current in an ideal, zero-resistance inductor is raised from zero to \( I \). The work done against its back-EMF:
options: is stored as magnetic field energy \( \tfrac12LI^2 \)
is dissipated as heat in the coil
is zero, since the coil has no resistance
questions.explanation:
The back-EMF opposes the increase (Lenz's law), so the source does work \( \int L I\,dI=\tfrac12LI^2 \).

This energy is stored in the magnetic field and returned when the current falls.
questions.hint: Back-EMF opposes the increase, so work is done.
distractor_logic: A zero-resistance coil cannot dissipate heat.
The back-EMF opposes the rising current, so work must be done even without resistance.
No significant radiation occurs; the energy stays in the field.

questions.question: A generator feeds a fixed resistor. If its rotation speed is doubled, the peak power dissipated in the resistor becomes:
questions.explanation:
\( \varepsilon_0=NBA\omega \) doubles.

Peak power \( =\dfrac{\varepsilon_0^2}{R} \), so it rises by \( 2^2=4 \); the extra power comes from extra mechanical work against the stronger retarding torque.
questions.hint: Power goes as EMF squared.
distractor_logic: Doubles the EMF but forgets that power goes as EMF squared.
Treats the peak EMF as \( NBA \), independent of \( \omega \).
Cubes the factor with no basis.

questions.question: As the current in a coil rises from 2 A to 5 A in 0.1 s, the flux linked with the coil rises from 0.2 Wb to 0.5 Wb. The average self-induced EMF is:
questions.explanation:
\( |\varepsilon|=\dfrac{\Delta(N\Phi)}{\Delta t}=\dfrac{0.3}{0.1}=3 \) V.

Check: \( L=\dfrac{0.2}{2}=0.1 \) H, and \( L\dfrac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}=0.1\times30=3 \) V.
questions.hint: Self-induction is Faraday's law for the coil's own flux.
distractor_logic: Divides the final flux linkage by the time instead of the change.
Uses the change in flux linkage but forgets to divide by the time.
Reports the rate of change of current as the EMF.

questions.question: A 0.5 H inductor carrying 4 A is disconnected from its source and connected across a resistor. The total heat produced in the resistor is:
options: It depends on the value of the resistance
questions.explanation:
The inductor's stored energy is \( \tfrac12LI^2=\tfrac12\times0.5\times16=4 \) J.

The back-EMF keeps the current flowing as it decays, and all this energy ends up as heat.
questions.hint: All stored energy becomes heat.
distractor_logic: Drops the \( \tfrac12 \) in \( \tfrac12LI^2 \).
Uses \( \tfrac12LI \) without squaring the current.
The resistance changes how fast the energy is released, not how much.

distractor_logic: A clockwise current would add to the growing flux, aiding the change.

questions.question: Two coaxial solenoids have the same length and area, with 500 and 1500 turns per metre. The first has \( L_1=2 \) mH. Their mutual inductance is:

questions.question: Pulling a solid aluminium sheet out of the gap of a strong magnet needs noticeably more force than pulling out a sheet with many slots cut across it. Why?
options: Larger eddy currents in the solid sheet produce a stronger force opposing its motion
The solid sheet is magnetised and attracted by the magnet
The slotted sheet has eddy currents that help pull it out
The solid sheet is heavier, and that alone explains the difference
questions.explanation:
Each part of the moving sheet has a motional EMF, driving eddy currents.

These currents feel a force opposing the motion (Lenz's law); slots break the current loops, so the drag is much smaller.
questions.hint: Slots cut the current paths.
distractor_logic: Aluminium is not appreciably magnetic; the force is from induced currents.
Eddy currents always oppose the motion; they never help it.
The force needed is felt only while the sheet moves in the field, so it is magnetic drag, not weight.

questions.question: A loop is pulled out of a uniform field at speed \( v \). If it is instead pulled out at \( 2v \), the charge that flows through it and the heat produced become:
questions.explanation:
Charge \( q=\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{R} \), independent of speed.

Heat \( =I^2Rt \) with \( I\propto v \) and \( t\propto\dfrac1v \), so heat \( \propto v \) and doubles.
questions.hint: Compare the charge formula with \( I^2Rt \).
distractor_logic: Charge \( =\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{R} \) does not depend on speed.
Charge is fixed by the flux change; heat grows only in proportion to \( v \).

\( \varepsilon=B_vlv=4\times10^{-5}\times20\times250=0.2 \) V.

questions.question: The current in coil 1 repeatedly ramps up from 0 to 2 A in 0.01 s and back down to 0 in 0.01 s. The mutual inductance with coil 2 is 0.05 H. The EMF in coil 2 is:
options: a square wave of magnitude 10 V, reversing sign every 0.01 s
a triangular wave of peak 0.1 V
a constant 10 V that never changes sign
zero, since the current returns to zero
questions.explanation:
\( \left|\dfrac{dI_1}{dt}\right|=\dfrac{2}{0.01}=200 \) A/s on each ramp.

\( |\varepsilon_2|=0.05\times200=10 \) V, with the sign flipping as the slope flips: a square wave.
questions.hint: EMF follows the slope of the current.
distractor_logic: Uses \( MI_1 \), which is the flux linkage, rather than \( M\dfrac{dI_1}{dt} \).
Misses that the slope reverses on the down-ramp, reversing the EMF.
The EMF depends on the rate of change, which is large even though the average current change over a cycle is zero.

Coil 2: \( M\dfrac{dI_1}{dt}=0.15\times20=3 \) V.

Check: \( k=\dfrac{0.15}{\sqrt{0.04}}=0.75 \), within range.

questions.question: The steady current in a coil is doubled. Its self-inductance and stored energy become:

questions.question: A long straight wire and a nearby rectangular loop have a mutual inductance of \( 2\ \mu\text{H} \). The wire's current rises at 500 A/s. The induced EMF in the loop, and the direction of current in the loop's side nearest the wire, are:
options: 1 mV; in the same direction as the wire's current
1 V; opposite to the wire's current
zero, since the loop is not connected to the wire
1 mV; opposite to the wire's current

\( |\varepsilon|=M\dfrac{dI}{dt}=2\times10^{-6}\times500=10^{-3} \) V \( =1 \) mV.

The flux through the loop is growing, so the induced current opposes it; the near side carries current opposite to the wire, and antiparallel currents repel.
questions.hint: Opposing an increase means repulsion.
distractor_logic: Parallel currents attract and would aid the flux increase, reversing Lenz's law.
Treats microhenry as millihenry, a factor of 1000 too large.
Coupling is magnetic; no connection is needed.

questions.question: Two coaxial solenoids have the same length and turns per metre, but the outer has four times the cross-sectional area of the inner. The coefficient of coupling is:

\( k=\dfrac{M}{\sqrt{L_{in}L_{out}}}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt4}=0.5 \).

questions.topic: Lenz's Law and Motional EMF: Direction, Induced Force, Power, and Energy Conservation
questions.question: A bar magnet falls vertically through a closed copper ring. Its acceleration while approaching the ring and while leaving it is:
options: less than \( g \) while approaching, greater than \( g \) while leaving
less than \( g \) in both cases
greater than \( g \) in both cases
questions.explanation:
Approaching, the ring opposes the growing flux by repelling the magnet.

Leaving, the ring opposes the falling flux by attracting it back.

Either way the force is upward, so the acceleration is below \( g \); the lost energy becomes heat in the ring, as with eddy-current braking.
questions.hint: Induced effects oppose the relative motion.
distractor_logic: The current reverses on leaving, but it then opposes the decrease, which still means pulling the magnet back.
Induced currents never speed the magnet up.
A closed ring carries induced currents that exert a retarding force.
